SECTION I
I	A working man, father of six, sits at the table in his small bungalow on the outskirts of Stoke-
on-Trent in the Midlands of England. He — let’s call him Mr H — takes a pencil and paper and
traces the outline of each of his hands. He then folds the paper and places it, along with a
descriptive note, in an envelope addressed to the Eugenics Society, 20 Grosvenor Gardens,
London, and ‘anxiously awaits reply’.
It is December 1930, and a campaign to legalise the surgical sterilisation of the ‘mentally
deficient’ is in full swing. Over the previous decade, thousands of people have already been
sterilised across various US states, under laws penned and promoted by eugenics campaigners.
Inspired, Britain’s Eugenics Society — whose 700-strong membership included medical doctors,
clergymen and leading scientists, such as the statistician R A Fisher and the biologist Julian
Huxley — is on the march, pumping out propaganda pamphlets and filling correspondence
sections of UK newspapers, magazines and medical journals. Eugenic sterilisation, they argue,
is safe, humane, and urgently necessary. Only decisive action can curtail the supposed
overzealous breeding of so-called ‘defectives’ and arrest the racial deterioration of the British
people. Moreover, and crucially amid the economic wreckage of the Great Depression, a
sterilisation programme promises to curb the spiralling costs of caring for those deemed
‘feebleminded’ in overburdened state institutions.
Historians know what happens next, or rather, what doesn’t. Unlike their counterparts in the
United States, Canada or, notoriously, Germany, British politicians proved unwilling to ratify
such extreme and targeted interventions into the lives and bodies of individual citizens. When
introduced into Parliament in the summer of 1931, the Eugenics Society-backed Sterilisation
Bill was defeated — 89 ‘ayes’ versus 167 ‘noes’ (130 of which came from Labour MPs who
opposed the Bill as anti-working class). The matter was never again put to the vote in
Westminster. A near miss. Fast-forward a decade and a half and, amid the fallout from the
Second World War and revelations of Nazi genocide, ‘eugenics’ would acquire toxic political
baggage. The Eugenics Society limped on through the postwar period but, as the credibility of
the wider movement crumbled, its mission necessarily evolved. [Word Count: 358]

people-support-eugenics-in-the-19380s

content.explanation: the passage shows that eugenic ideas were not marginal or absurd at the time, but were supported by highly respected institutions and public voices. The author’s concern is precisely that elite endorsement made such coercive measures appear legitimate and administratively reasonable.

content.passageText:
Til.	Men have started sewing up a storm, driving a culture shift that challenges the traditional
notion of sewing as a “women’s hobby”. The COVID pandemic drove a resurgence in home
economics, with many people — including many men — picking up skills such as sewing and
knitting. This trend has since grown, even as lockdowns have ended. And it disrupts the
dominant narrative that men stick to stereotypical masculine identities — particularly in rural
Australia, where social pressure to behave a certain way can feel amplified. The term
“performative male” has been used to describe a sub-group of men who try really hard to
appear “non-masculine” — usually for the purpose of attracting women. Is picking up the
sewing just another performative male trick? www.lawpreptutorial.com
The research suggests not. Instead, it reveals a subculture of men who are genuine fashion
enthusiasts taking up the skill. Globally, men’s sewing groups have also been established as a
way to foster community and improve mental health. Gen Z’s members in particular are not
shying away from personalising their style — and finding ways to customise their wardrobes on
a budget. These young men are not as strongly influenced by trends flowing down from
runways. Instead, they leverage social media platforms such as TikTok and Instagram to share
their passion and influence others, bringing more young men into the fold. The rise of men
mending and sewing clothes has also been linked to broader societal awareness of
sustainability and overconsumption issues. While sewing has long been (and arguably still is)
viewed as a typically feminine pursuit, there is some historic precedent for the rise of sewing
among men today. Throughout history, tailoring and suit-making have been seen as acceptable
professions for men — and still are in many cultures such as in Pakistan, South Korea, Italy
and Hong Kong. [Word Count: 297]

womans-hobby-why-more-men-are-picking-up-sewing-and-why-you-should-too-271191

content.passageText:
IV.	Many Years Later as he faced the firing squad, Colonel Aureliano Buendia was to remember
that distant afternoon when his father took him to discover ice. At that time Macondo was a
village of twenty adobe houses, built on the bank of a river of clear water that ran along a bed
of polished stones, which were white and enormous, like prehistoric eggs. The world was so
recent that many things lacked names, and in order to indicate them it was necessary to point.
Every year during the month of March a family of ragged gypsies would set up their tents near
the village, and with a great uproar of pipes and kettledrums they would display new
inventions. First they brought the magnet. A heavy gypsy with an untamed beard and sparrow
hands, who introduced himself as Melquiades, put on a bold public demonstration of what he
himself called the eighth wonder of the learned alchemists of Macedonia. He went from house
to house dragging two metal ingots and everybody was amazed to see pots, pans, tongs, and
braziers tumble down from their places and beams creak from the desperation of nails and
screws trying to emerge, and even objects that had been lost for a long time appeared from
where they had been searched for most and went dragging along in turbulent confusion behind
Melquiades’ magical irons. “Things have a life of their own,” the gypsy proclaimed with a harsh
accent. “It’s simply a matter of waking up their souls.” José Arcadio Buendia, whose unbridled
imagination always went beyond the genius of nature and even beyond miracles and magic,
thought that it would be possible to make use of that useless invention to extract gold from the
bowels of the earth. Melquiades, who was an honest man, warned him: “It won’t work for that.”
But José Arcadio Buendia at that time did not believe in the honesty of gypsies, so he traded
his mule and a pair of goats for the two magnetized ingots. Ursula Iguaran, his wife, who
relied on those animals to increase their poor domestic holdings, was unable to dissuade him.
“Very soon we'll have gold, enough and more to pave the floors of the house,” her husband
replied. For several months he worked hard to demonstrate the truth of his idea. He explored
every inch of the region, even the riverbed, dragging the two iron ingots along and reciting
Melquiades’ incantation aloud. [Word Count: 407]
Source: Extracted with: One Hundred Years of Solitude by Gabriel Garcia Marquez

VI.	Tran stated that it has good contact with India over the passage of ships from the Strait of
Hormuz and wants to help New Delhi with navigation. It also denied charging a toll for Indian
tankers while transiting through the Strait of Hormuz. Iranian ambassador to India,
Mohammad Fathali, in a press briefing, also stated that Iran and India share the same fate
and interests, and the two nations maintain strong ties amidst the challenging times. He
further stressed that Iran never charged India for the passage of its ships through the Hormuz
after US President Donald Trump vowed to block passage for vessels making payments to
Tran.
New Delhi, on various occasions, has also denied ever paying toll for the passage of its nine
ships through the waterway. It has secured nine liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) tankers since
Tran has barred the passage of tankers, while 15 India-flagged ships remain stuck in the
Persian Gulf. Detailing the further navigation of Indian tankers from the strait, the

ambassador stated that Iran wants to help India navigate the passage of tankers. Iran is
ready to sell its oil to any country that wants to purchase it. Notably, about half of India’s
crude oil and LPG supplies pass through the Strait of Hormuz. So far 45,000 kg of medicines
have been shipped to Iran in two batches since the war broke out. The latest batch will be sent
in a Mahaan air flight from Delhi to Mashhad for nationwide distribution. [Word Count: 248]

VII. Senior Advocate Menaka Guruswamy was sworn into the Rajya Sabha as a Trinamool
Congress member. Guruswamy, 51, with a legacy of defending civil liberties, sees her move
into the political arena as the next logical step in a career defined by challenging the status
quo. She views the legislature fundamentally as a deliberative body, rather than a space for
show of muscle. Her primary legislative agenda, she says, will be safeguarding the
Constitution, ensuring that new Bills are not bulldozed through. Thoughtful legislation, she
says, requires scrutiny by parliamentary committees and stakeholder consultation.
Guruswamy sees the Opposition’s role in this context as one involved in checking the
constitutional calibre of new legislation. Earlier this year, while representing the party in
petitions relating to the Enforcement Directorate’s raids on I-PAC, the political consultancy
that works for the TMC, Guruswamy caught attention for her strong objection to Additional
Solicitor General S V Raju referring to Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee by her name. In the
legal sphere, Guruswamy enjoys a formidable reputation in constitutional, commercial and
white-collar criminal law. In 2019, the Supreme Court designated her as a Senior Advocate.
Last month, she secured from the apex court permanent commissions and pensions for eligible
women officers in the armed forces. She is slated to argue for women’s entry into the
Sabarimala temple before the Constitution Bench that is currently hearing the matter. In
2018, she was part of the team that persuaded the Supreme Court to strike it down. Following
the verdict, she and her co-counsel, Arundhati Katju, publicly announced their relationship.
[Word Count: 259]

IX.	Shri Suman Bery, Vice-Chairman, NITI Aayog, and Smt. Nidhi Chhibber, Chief Executive
Officer (CEO), NITI Aayog, released the Fiscal Health Index 2026 in New Delhi today. It was
released in the distinguished presence of other senior officials. www.lawpreptutorial.com
The Fiscal Health Index provides a comprehensive and comparable assessment of the fiscal
performance of Indian states. The Index has been designed as a data-driven framework to
evaluate fiscal soundness, guide reforms, and promote evidence-based fiscal policymaking
across states. At a time when global public finances are under mounting pressure the
sustainability of sub-national finances has assumed increasing importance. In this context,
robust fiscal management at all levels of government has become essential to maintaining
macroeconomic stability and supporting long-term development.
In India, state governments play a critical role in the country’s fiscal architecture. States now
account for nearly one-third of India’s general government debt, making their fiscal trajectory
central to national fiscal sustainability. Given the scale of state expenditure responsibilities

and their role in delivering key public services, systematic assessment of state finances is
essential to ensure fiscal discipline, efficient resource allocation, and long-term macroeconomic
stability. The Fiscal Health Index seeks to provide such an assessment by enabling
benchmarking across states and identifying areas for improvement. The report highlights
several policy priorities for strengthening fiscal health across states. These include enhancing
revenue mobilisation and strengthening state own-tax capacity; rationalising committed
expenditures to restore fiscal flexibility; improving the composition and quality of capital
expenditure; and adopting medium-term fiscal planning frameworks to manage deficits and
debt trajectories more effectively. [Word Count: 255]

content.passageText:
SECTION III
xX.	A contract of indemnity is a contract of protection by which one party undertakes to save the
other from loss. Halsbury describes indemnity as a contract, express or implied, to keep a
person indemnified against loss, independent of whether a third person makes default. Black’s
Law Dictionary also explains indemnity as a right by which the entire loss is shifted from one
who is only technically or secondarily liable to another who is primarily responsible. The
Indian Contract Act, 1872 defines it in Section 124 as a contract by which one party promises
to save the other from loss caused by the conduct of the promisor himself or by the conduct of
any other person. The person giving the indemnity is the indemnifier, and the person
protected is the indemnity-holder or indemnified. The contract may be express or implied, as
seen in Adamson v. Jarvis, Secretary of State v. Bank of India Ltd., and Starkey v. Bank of
England, where courts recognised implied promises of indemnity from the circumstances and
conduct of parties.
The essential features of a contract of indemnity are that it must be a valid contract under the
Indian Contract Act, its main object must be protection from loss, its terms may be express or
implied, and it involves only two parties, unlike a contract of guarantee. It is contingent in
nature because liability arises on the happening of a specified event causing loss. Insurance
contracts are generally contracts of indemnity except life insurance, because life insurance
does not depend on proof of an actual quantified loss. As held in New India Assurance Co. Ltd.
v. State Trading Corporation of India, almost all insurance other than life and personal
accident insurance are contracts of indemnity. A third party cannot sue the indemnifier
because of the doctrine of privity, as observed in National Petroleum Company v. Popat Lal
Mulji.
Section 125 sets out the rights of the indemnity-holder. He may recover all damages he is
compelled to pay in a suit to which the indemnity applies, all costs incurred in bringing or
defending such a suit if he acted prudently and within authority, and all sums paid under a
reasonable compromise made in good faith. The indemnifier, though not expressly given rights
in the Act, enjoys subrogation rights after making payment. In Gajanan Moreshwar v.
Moreshwar Madan, the Bombay High Court held that once the indemnified’s liability becomes
absolute, the indemnifier must fulfil the promise without waiting for actual payment. This
modern rule departs from the old English view that actual loss must first be suffered. Cases
like Osman Jamal and Sons Ltd. v. Gopal Purushottam and The New India Assurance Co. Ltd.
v. State Trading Corporation of India Ltd. support the principle that indemnity becomes
enforceable as soon as liability becomes absolute. However, indemnity will not cover unlawful
or intentional wrongful acts, as shown in Sheikh Meherulla v. Sariatulla and Geismar v. Sun
Alliance and London Insurance Ltd. Thus, contracts of indemnity remain an important legal
device for risk allocation, financial security, and protection against liability.

http://student.manupatra.com/Academic/Abk/Law-of-Contract-and-Specific-
Relief/Chapter9.htm

A shipping company enters into an indemnity arrangement with a port operator to cover losses
arising from mishandling of containers. A container owner, whose goods are damaged, directly
sues the port operator’s indemnifier for compensation, arguing the indemnity “shifts the entire

Cargo owner can sue indemnifier directly, because indemnity shifts the entire loss and
privity never blocks enforcement when third parties suffer harm.

Cargo owner can sue indemnifier only if he proves malice, because indemnity resembles
tort and requires wrongful intent before courts grant recovery.

Cargo owner cannot sue indemnifier because of the doctrine of privity, so only the
indemnity-holder may enforce the promise against him directly.

Cargo owner cannot sue indemnifier because indemnity is void without court registration,
so absence of stamp and filing defeats enforcement by anyone.

A start-up signs an indemnity clause promising to protect its CFO against any penalty the
regulators may impose for an internal compliance failure. A whistleblower complaint is filed,
but no notice has been issued and no penalty proceedings have begun. The CFO demands
immediate payment into escrow, saying the indemnity is "for protection" and uncertainty is
enough. The company refuses, saying the indemnity obligation is triggered only if a specified
loss event actually happens.
How should the timing of liability be understood?

The indemnifier must pay immediately because indemnity is absolute, and contingency is
irrelevant once promise is signed, even if no loss event occurs.

The indemnifier must pay immediately because liability arises whenever the indemnity-
holder feels insecure, so court orders pre-emptive reimbursement to avoid future disputes.

Indemnifier need not pay yet because no regulatory notice has been issued and no penalty
proceedings have begun, so the specified loss event that would trigger the indemnity
obligation has not occurred.

Indemnifier pays only when liability arises on the happening of a specified event causing
loss, so payment is premature before the specified loss event occurs.

refuses to pay, arguing the family has not produced bills or evidence of an “actual quantified

quantification is mandatory.
Which conclusion best follows?

Insurer cannot demand proof of quantified loss, because life insurance does not depend on
proof of an actual quantified loss, and pays on death.

Insurer can demand proof of quantified loss, because all insurance is indemnity, and
claimant must show actual monetary damage before any payout is allowed.

Insurer can deny payout because indemnity arises only after liability becomes absolute, so
without court decree of loss, the policy remains unenforceable.

Insurer must reimburse only medical expenses, because life policies cover only proved
hospital bills, and do not pay any fixed sum upon death.

A construction company indemnifies its architect against litigation arising from design
allegations. A client sues the architect and demands damages. The architect, acting on legal
advice, enters a settlement that is reasonable in the circumstances and made in good faith,
avoiding a larger exposure. The indemnifier refuses reimbursement, arguing that only court-
decreed damages are covered and settlements are “voluntary.” The architect claims indemnity
includes certain payments made by compromise.
Which claim most directly fits the indemnity-holder’s recovery rights?

The indemnity-holder may recover only court-awarded damages, and cannot claim
compromise amounts, even if settlement was reasonable, because no decree exists.

The indemnity-holder may recover costs only, because indemnity covers litigation
expenses, but compromise sums are personal choices and remain unpaid by indemnifier
alone.

The indemnity-holder may recover all sums paid under a reasonable compromise made in
good faith, if compromise was within authority and prudent too.

The indemnity-holder may recover compromise sums only if indemnifier signed the
settlement deed, because good faith alone never permits reimbursement in law.

A bank guarantees a borrower’s liability to a vendor and receives a separate indemnity from
the borrower promising to protect the bank against that vendor claim. The vendor sues the
bank, and the court passes a final decree making the bank’s liability fixed and enforceable.
Before the bank actually pays the vendor, it demands that the borrower deposit the decree
amount under the indemnity. The borrower argues indemnity is payable only after the bank
actually pays.
Who has the stronger position on timing?

The indemnifier can wait until indemnity-holder actually pays, because indemnity is
enforceable only after real loss is suffered, not earlier in any case ever.

The indemnifier must pay only if third party sues him directly, because indemnity cannot
be claimed by holder until privity is removed fully.

The indemnifier must pay when liability is contingent, because mere apprehension is
enough, and the indemnity-holder may demand advance payment before any claim arises.

Once the indemnified’s liability becomes absolute, the indemnifier must fulfil the promise
without waiting for actual payment, so the indemnity-holder can claim immediately.

XI.	Belligerent occupation refers to a situation in which the armed forces of one state seize and
administer control over the territory of another sovereign state during armed conflict or its
aftermath. The control is not meant to be permanent; rather, it is provisional and continues
only for the period of military necessity or until the conflict is resolved. A territory is
considered under belligerent occupation when it is under the effective control of a hostile
army, meaning there must be actual administration and “boots on the ground,” and when the
control is temporary in character rather than an annexation. The occupying power is bound by
international law and must protect the rights and welfare of the civilian population.
Belligerent occupation is therefore distinct from annexation or colonialism, because
sovereignty is not lawfully transferred to the occupier.
The legal framework of belligerent occupation is primarily found in the Hague Conventions of
1907, the Geneva Conventions of 1949, especially the Fourth Geneva Convention, and
customary international law. Article 42 of the Fourth Hague Convention states that a territory
is occupied when it is actually placed under the authority of a hostile army, while Article 43
obliges the occupying power to restore and maintain public order and safety and to respect the
existing laws of the occupied territory as far as possible. The Fourth Geneva Convention adds
humanitarian protections, especially for civilians, including the prohibition on forced transfer
or deportation under Article 49. The law emphasises that occupation is only an interim
arrangement and must not become a method of permanently displacing sovereignty. Scholars
such as Eyal Benvenisti have explained that the modern law of occupation rests on the
principle of the inalienability of sovereignty, meaning that military control cannot lawfully
extinguish the sovereign rights of the occupied state.
History provides several illustrations of belligerent occupation. After the First World War, the
Occupied Enemy Territory Administration (OETA) governed parts of the Middle East from

1917 to 1920 as a temporary regime. After the Second World War, Allied-occupied Germany
(1945-1949) was administered militarily until sovereignty could be gradually restored. In the
contemporary era, one of the most debated examples is the Israeli control over Palestinian
territories, which the United Nations has characterised as belligerent occupation. UN Security
Council Resolutions 242 and 338 support the principle of “Land for Peace,” under which

State R occupies a border strip and orders all civilians living near the frontier to board buses to
“temporary camps” far away. Families are told they cannot return until “security conditions improve,”

Forced transfer of civilians is prohibited so relocating residents for security corridor violates
humanitarian protections of occupation law very clearly.

Forced transfer of civilians is prohibited but relocation becomes lawful if consent is presumed from
silence and compensation offered in law.

Forced transfer is lawful if occupier offers compensation so security relocation with payment
complies with humanitarian duties in law.

Forced transfer is lawful when civilians are moved within same territory so only deportation abroad
is prohibited by law.

Sovereignty is not lawfully transferred, so occupier must withdraw within twenty-four hours and

content.passageText:
XII. The doctrine of jus necessitatis, or necessity, has deep historical roots and recognises that in
certain exceptional situations, an act which would otherwise be unlawful may be justified if it
is done to prevent a greater harm. Medieval jurists such as Henry de Bracton stated that “that
which is otherwise not lawful is made lawful by necessity,” and Roman law reflected the same
idea in the maxim “Necessitas non habet legem’, meaning necessity knows no law. The
doctrine therefore developed as a legal justification for urgent acts done for survival,
preservation, or prevention of serious harm. In modern terms, jus necessitatis means a person
may do something technically illegal if it is necessary to avoid a more serious injury or danger.
A common example is breaking into a house to rescue a child trapped in a fire: the trespass is
excused because the saving of life is the higher value.

In common law, the doctrine of necessity is mainly used as a defence, especially in criminal
law, though it has also appeared in administrative and constitutional law. It is supported by
the maxims “Quod necessitas non habet legem” and “Necessitas vincit legem”, the latter
meaning necessity triumphs over law. In India, the doctrine is codified in Section 81 of the
Indian Penal Code, 1860, which states that an act likely to cause harm is not an offence if it is
done without criminal intention, in good faith, and for the purpose of preventing or avoiding
other harm to person or property. This Section 81 requires two essential conditions: absence of
criminal intent and good faith, along with the idea that the harm prevented must be greater
than the harm caused. For example, destroying one house to stop a fire from spreading to an
entire neighbourhood may be justified under Section 81.
Indian courts have recognised this doctrine in cases such as Gullapalli Nageswara Rao v.
APSRTC (1958) and Election Commission of India v. Dr. Subramaniam Swamy (1996), the
latter stressing that the doctrine should apply only in cases of absolute necessity.
International cases also illustrate its limits. In Regina v. Dudley and Stephens (1884),
necessity was rejected as a defence to murder, while United States v. Holmes (1842) and Rex
v. Bourne (1938) show that it may apply under strict conditions. The doctrine, however, is
limited by requirements of proportionality, good faith, absence of alternatives, and absolute
necessity. Though criticised for possible misuse, ambiguity, and erosion of legal certainty, it
remains an important legal principle for dealing with extraordinary situations where rigid
obedience to law would produce greater injustice.

into lawful act, and necessity does not matter here.

XII. The doctrine of jus necessitatis, or necessity, has deep historical roots and recognises that in
certain exceptional situations, an act which would otherwise be unlawful may be justified if it
is done to prevent a greater harm. Medieval jurists such as Henry de Bracton stated that “that
which is otherwise not lawful is made lawful by necessity,” and Roman law reflected the same
idea in the maxim “Necessitas non habet legem’, meaning necessity knows no law. The
doctrine therefore developed as a legal justification for urgent acts done for survival,
preservation, or prevention of serious harm. In modern terms, jus necessitatis means a person
may do something technically illegal if it is necessary to avoid a more serious injury or danger.
A common example is breaking into a house to rescue a child trapped in a fire: the trespass is
excused because the saving of life is the higher value.

In common law, the doctrine of necessity is mainly used as a defence, especially in criminal
law, though it has also appeared in administrative and constitutional law. It is supported by
the maxims “Quod necessitas non habet legem” and “Necessitas vincit legem”, the latter
meaning necessity triumphs over law. In India, the doctrine is codified in Section 81 of the
Indian Penal Code, 1860, which states that an act likely to cause harm is not an offence if it is
done without criminal intention, in good faith, and for the purpose of preventing or avoiding
other harm to person or property. This Section 81 requires two essential conditions: absence of
criminal intent and good faith, along with the idea that the harm prevented must be greater
than the harm caused. For example, destroying one house to stop a fire from spreading to an
entire neighbourhood may be justified under Section 81.
Indian courts have recognised this doctrine in cases such as Gullapalli Nageswara Rao v.
APSRTC (1958) and Election Commission of India v. Dr. Subramaniam Swamy (1996), the
latter stressing that the doctrine should apply only in cases of absolute necessity.
International cases also illustrate its limits. In Regina v. Dudley and Stephens (1884),
necessity was rejected as a defence to murder, while United States v. Holmes (1842) and Rex
v. Bourne (1938) show that it may apply under strict conditions. The doctrine, however, is
limited by requirements of proportionality, good faith, absence of alternatives, and absolute
necessity. Though criticised for possible misuse, ambiguity, and erosion of legal certainty, it
remains an important legal principle for dealing with extraordinary situations where rigid
obedience to law would produce greater injustice.

to the district headquarters. The election authority announces a one-day extension of the filing deadline

argues that statutory timelines cannot be altered. The authority replies that the decision was compelled
by necessity and that the doctrine should operate only where absolute necessity exists.
Which conclusion best applies this limitation?

Upheld because necessity always excuses illegality, and courts never review emergency choices once
officials claim public interest.

Struck because necessity applies only to criminal cases, and election administration cannot ever use
necessity for procedural changes.

Upheld because necessity knows no law, so statutory deadlines may be ignored whenever there is
inconvenience or delay in logistics.

Upheld only where absolute necessity exists, so extraordinary flood justifying limited extension fits
necessity’s strict threshold.

pleads necessity, saying he acted in good faith, without criminal intent, and that the harm prevented

How should the court evaluate his defence?

Defence fails because any harmful act is an offence, and preventing harm can never justify causing
harm to property here.

The defence succeeds because Section 81 requires absence of criminal intent and good faith, and the
harm prevented must exceed harm caused.

Defence succeeds because intention to save someone automatically excuses any damage, even if
alternatives existed and the risk was avoidable.

Defence fails because good faith is irrelevant, and only the actor’s personal fear matters, not
proportionality of harms.

A trekking group is trapped when a sudden landslide blocks the only marked trail and an avalanche
warning is issued. To reach safety before nightfall, the guide cuts a locked fence and leads hikers
through a private orchard, trampling saplings and breaking irrigation pipes. The owner files a complaint
for trespass and damage. The guide claims necessity but evidence shows an alternative public route
existed, though it would take two extra hours.
How should the necessity defence be assessed under the stated limits?

Defence succeeds because any emergency automatically justifies illegality, and proportionality or
alternatives do not matter once danger exists.

Defence fails because necessity never applies outside murder, so property damage and trespass can
never be excused in law.

Defence succeeds only if proportionality, good faith, absence of alternatives, and absolute necessity
are shown, so evidence matters.

Defence fails because rescuers must wait for police permission, and self-help is never allowed even to
prevent serious harm.

After a shipwreck, four survivors drift for days without food or rescue, facing extreme starvation.
Believing all will die, two survivors agree to kill the weakest member and consume his body to
survive. They are rescued the next morning and prosecuted for intentional killing. They claim
necessity: the act was the only way to avoid the greater harm of everyone dying. Assuming these
facts are proved, which legal position best matches the passage principle on necessity?
options:
Defence succeeds because necessity triumphs over law, so killing one to save others is lawful
when survival is at stake.

Defence fails because necessity was rejected as a defence to murder, so intentional killing
cannot be justified by survival claims.

Defence succeeds because absence of alternatives always excuses homicide, and courts must
prefer utilitarian outcomes over legal prohibitions.

Defence fails only if killing was malicious, so if done in good faith and fairly, murder becomes
excusable necessity.

During a rapidly spreading warehouse fire, Ritu, the site supervisor, orders workers to pull down a
neighbour's wooden shed to create a firebreak. The shed is destroyed, but the fire stops and a dense

property. Ritu argues she acted in good faith, without any criminal intention, and solely to prevent

Which outcome best follows on these facts?

Defence fails because the act was deliberate and targeted at another's property; even if the

consent.

Defence fails because destroying property is always criminal mischief, and necessity never
excuses deliberate destruction of another's house.

Defence succeeds only if the act was done without criminal intention, in good faith, and to
prevent other harm.

Defence fails because the harm caused must equal or exceed the harm prevented before
necessity can apply, and here only one shed was lost against a neighbourhood saved.

XI. The Principles of Natural Justice are fundamental legal doctrines that ensure fairness,
impartiality, and reasoned decision-making in judicial, quasi-judicial, and administrative
proceedings. Rooted in moral principles, Roman law, and common law traditions, they protect
individuals from arbitrary action by requiring due process in decision-making. Their historical
basis can be traced to ancient Greek and Roman thought, medieval jurists such as Henry de
Bracton, and even religious narratives that emphasised giving a person an opportunity to explain
before punishment. In modern Indian law, the Supreme Court in Mohinder Singh Gill v. Chief
Election Commissioner affirmed that fairness is essential in all forms of state decision-making. The
three core principles of natural justice are the hearing rule (audi alteram partem), the bias rule
(nemo judex in causa sua), and the requirement of a reasoned decision or speaking order.

The first principle, audi alteram partem, means that no person should be condemned without being
given a fair opportunity to be heard. It requires proper notice, a chance to present evidence and
arguments, the opportunity to cross-examine where necessary, and adjudication by an unbiased
authority. The second principle, nemo judex in causa sua, ensures that no one should be a judge in
their own cause. This rule guards against different forms of bias such as personal bias, pecuniary
bias, subject matter bias, departmental bias, policy notion bias, and bias due to stubbornness. The
third principle requires that every decision must be supported by reasons. A speaking order
promotes transparency, prevents arbitrariness, enables appeal or judicial review, and strengthens
accountability. These principles have become vital in administrative law, especially after Maneka
Gandhi v. Union of India (1978), where the Supreme Court emphasised that fairness,
reasonableness, and justice are essential in procedures affecting rights and liberties.
Although natural justice is fundamental, it is not absolute and admits certain exceptions. It may be
excluded or modified in emergency situations, where immediate action is necessary for public
safety; by express statutory exclusion, where legislation validly limits procedural safeguards;
where disclosure would prejudice public interest, such as matters of national security; where
prompt action is needed; or where it is impracticable to hold a hearing or appeal. It may also be
relaxed in purely administrative matters, where no substantial legal right is affected, or where no
right of the person is infringed. Courts may also overlook procedural defects if they would have
made no difference to the outcome, or where the decision-maker acted in good faith without fault.
Even in such cases, however, these exceptions must be applied cautiously so that fairness,
transparency, and the protection of individual rights remain central to the legal process.

not be supported by reasons.

Cancellation invalid only if hearing denied; requirement of reasons applies only to judicial
judgments, not administrative decisions.

brief rejection is acceptable for public interest sometimes.

Cancellation invalid because every decision must be supported by reasons; a speaking
order enables review and prevents arbitrariness for fairness.

that the committee chair’s spouse owns shares in Firm Z, and the chair never disclosed this

content.passageText:
XI. The Principles of Natural Justice are fundamental legal doctrines that ensure fairness,
impartiality, and reasoned decision-making in judicial, quasi-judicial, and administrative
proceedings. Rooted in moral principles, Roman law, and common law traditions, they protect
individuals from arbitrary action by requiring due process in decision-making. Their historical
basis can be traced to ancient Greek and Roman thought, medieval jurists such as Henry de
Bracton, and even religious narratives that emphasised giving a person an opportunity to explain
before punishment. In modern Indian law, the Supreme Court in Mohinder Singh Gill v. Chief
Election Commissioner affirmed that fairness is essential in all forms of state decision-making. The
three core principles of natural justice are the hearing rule (audi alteram partem), the bias rule
(nemo judex in causa sua), and the requirement of a reasoned decision or speaking order.

The first principle, audi alteram partem, means that no person should be condemned without being
given a fair opportunity to be heard. It requires proper notice, a chance to present evidence and
arguments, the opportunity to cross-examine where necessary, and adjudication by an unbiased
authority. The second principle, nemo judex in causa sua, ensures that no one should be a judge in
their own cause. This rule guards against different forms of bias such as personal bias, pecuniary
bias, subject matter bias, departmental bias, policy notion bias, and bias due to stubbornness. The
third principle requires that every decision must be supported by reasons. A speaking order
promotes transparency, prevents arbitrariness, enables appeal or judicial review, and strengthens
accountability. These principles have become vital in administrative law, especially after Maneka
Gandhi v. Union of India (1978), where the Supreme Court emphasised that fairness,
reasonableness, and justice are essential in procedures affecting rights and liberties.
Although natural justice is fundamental, it is not absolute and admits certain exceptions. It may be
excluded or modified in emergency situations, where immediate action is necessary for public
safety; by express statutory exclusion, where legislation validly limits procedural safeguards;
where disclosure would prejudice public interest, such as matters of national security; where
prompt action is needed; or where it is impracticable to hold a hearing or appeal. It may also be
relaxed in purely administrative matters, where no substantial legal right is affected, or where no
right of the person is infringed. Courts may also overlook procedural defects if they would have
made no difference to the outcome, or where the decision-maker acted in good faith without fault.
Even in such cases, however, these exceptions must be applied cautiously so that fairness,
transparency, and the protection of individual rights remain central to the legal process.

exceptions in any proceedings.

XIV. The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 marked a significant shift in Indian
law by recognising that violence within the home is not merely a private or personal matter, but a
legal wrong requiring enforceable remedies. Before this legislation, women facing abuse in
domestic relationships often had to depend on limited criminal provisions, such as cruelty under
matrimonial or penal law, or pursue separate civil proceedings for residence, maintenance, or
custody. The 2005 Act changed this position by creating a specialised legal framework that treats
domestic violence as a rights-based issue connected with dignity, bodily integrity, residence, and
security within the household.
A major feature of the Act is the broad statutory meaning of domestic violence. It is not confined to
physical assault or bodily injury. The law also covers sexual abuse, verbal and emotional abuse,
and economic abuse. Economic abuse includes deprivation of financial resources, disposal of
household assets, denial of maintenance, and restricting access to property or necessities to which
the aggrieved woman is entitled. Because of this broad definition, conduct that may not amount to
visible physical violence can still fall within the scope of the Act if it harms the woman’s safety,
well-being, dignity, or ability to live with security.
The Act applies to an aggrieved woman who is, or has been, in a domestic relationship with the
respondent. A domestic relationship includes relationships by marriage, blood, adoption, or a
relationship in the nature of marriage, provided the parties live or have lived together in a shared
household. Therefore, the protection is not confined only to legally wedded wives; it may also
extend to mothers, sisters, widows, and women in certain non-formal domestic arrangements, if the
statutory conditions are satisfied. www.lawpreptutorial.com
Another important principle is that the Act provides mainly civil remedies, though it is supported
by criminal procedure and enforcement. The Magistrate may grant protection orders, residence
orders, monetary relief, custody orders, and compensation. The law specifically recognises a
woman’s right to reside in the shared household, irrespective of ownership or title. It also imposes

duties on police officers, Magistrates, Protection Officers, service providers, shelter homes, and
medical facilities to assist the aggrieved person. Thus, the Act reflects the legal principle that
domestic violence is not outside the concern of law, and that the State must provide immediate,
practical, and effective remedies to secure a violence-free domestic environment.
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from,
https://repository.nls.ac.in/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1083&context=nlsir

Shalini’s partner never hits her, but he constantly humiliates her in front of relatives, monitors her
phone, and threatens to throw her out at night if she speaks to her parents. He also forces her to
sleep in the kitchen and denies her access to the bedroom, saying she is “not worthy.” When she
seeks relief, the respondent argues that without visible physical injuries the law cannot intervene.
Shalini argues that the harm is about dignity, residence, and security in the household.
What is the most defensible view?
options:
Relief denied because without bruises there is no legally cognisable harm, so dignity and
residence concerns are irrelevant.

Relief granted because any marital dispute is a rights issue, and courts must intervene to
protect feelings always at once.

Relief granted because the framework treats domestic violence as rights-based, linked with
dignity, bodily integrity, residence, and security at home.

Relief denied because only divorce courts can address residence and money issues, and criminal
courts handle assaults alone.

never legal wrongs here.

regardless of impact on her life always alone.

No, because civil remedies apply only after criminal conviction; without police charge-sheet, the
court cannot act at this stage.

Rupa, married for eight years, is repeatedly slapped and threatened at home when she
questions unexplained withdrawals from the joint account. One evening, her husband locks
her in a room, takes her phone, and warns she will be thrown out if she approaches anyone.
When Rupa goes to the police station, the duty officer refuses to record anything, saying "these
are private family issues." Rupa seeks immediate protection and residence-related relief
through a Magistrate.
What position best fits the framework described?
options:
Home disputes remain private matters; courts intervene only after criminal conviction, so
immediate civil relief is unavailable.

Violence within the home is a legal wrong requiring enforceable remedies, not merely a
private matter.

The law addresses only public violence; domestic incidents must be handled by family
elders, not courts.

A Magistrate can grant protection or residence relief only after the police formally register

content.passageText:
XIV. The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 marked a significant shift in Indian
law by recognising that violence within the home is not merely a private or personal matter, but a
legal wrong requiring enforceable remedies. Before this legislation, women facing abuse in
domestic relationships often had to depend on limited criminal provisions, such as cruelty under
matrimonial or penal law, or pursue separate civil proceedings for residence, maintenance, or
custody. The 2005 Act changed this position by creating a specialised legal framework that treats
domestic violence as a rights-based issue connected with dignity, bodily integrity, residence, and
security within the household.
A major feature of the Act is the broad statutory meaning of domestic violence. It is not confined to
physical assault or bodily injury. The law also covers sexual abuse, verbal and emotional abuse,
and economic abuse. Economic abuse includes deprivation of financial resources, disposal of
household assets, denial of maintenance, and restricting access to property or necessities to which
the aggrieved woman is entitled. Because of this broad definition, conduct that may not amount to
visible physical violence can still fall within the scope of the Act if it harms the woman’s safety,
well-being, dignity, or ability to live with security.
The Act applies to an aggrieved woman who is, or has been, in a domestic relationship with the
respondent. A domestic relationship includes relationships by marriage, blood, adoption, or a
relationship in the nature of marriage, provided the parties live or have lived together in a shared
household. Therefore, the protection is not confined only to legally wedded wives; it may also
extend to mothers, sisters, widows, and women in certain non-formal domestic arrangements, if the
statutory conditions are satisfied. www.lawpreptutorial.com
Another important principle is that the Act provides mainly civil remedies, though it is supported
by criminal procedure and enforcement. The Magistrate may grant protection orders, residence
orders, monetary relief, custody orders, and compensation. The law specifically recognises a
woman’s right to reside in the shared household, irrespective of ownership or title. It also imposes

duties on police officers, Magistrates, Protection Officers, service providers, shelter homes, and
medical facilities to assist the aggrieved person. Thus, the Act reflects the legal principle that
domestic violence is not outside the concern of law, and that the State must provide immediate,
practical, and effective remedies to secure a violence-free domestic environment.

court.

content.passageText:
SECTION IV
XV. If you've ever felt like you can't get ahead in life because there is only so much success to go
around, then you've experienced conflict theory in motion. Conflict theory is the belief that
people and systems are naturally in conflict and competition with each other for limited
resources. The conflict theory also suggests that people with power will do what they can do to
keep that power. German philosopher Karl Marx is considered the father of this theory, but
others have expanded on it. We'll discuss what conflict theory is in depth, how the idea has
developed and changed over time, how it relates to other sociological theories, and whether or
not it's still relevant to life today. Even though the term might sound a little complex, conflict
theory is a straightforward idea and it can be used to explain numerous elements of our lives,
such as social classes and wealth inequality. People often think of this theory in terms of why
war and other major conflicts take place, but we can also think about it in our everyday lives.
Conflict theory is based on a few principles: That we have a limited amount of resources in our
world, that humans operate out of self-interest, and that conflict can't be avoided within and
between social groups. It's considered the opposite of an idea called functionalism, which
claims that society will naturally work together for the greater good and every individual
serves a function towards that. This theory is taught in sociology courses, and its principles
since Marx presented them have been broadened over the years to include explanations for
war and racial inequality. The idea that we all have to compete is central to conflict theory. We
see this play out, in ways such as "people competing for a limited number of jobs that pay well
and have good benefits, or for a limited supply of affordable housing in a desirable area." In
this competition, who performs a function best does not innately lead them to achieve success.
These issues arise from there not being enough of these necessities to accommodate everyone
in society and we know that decisions about who gets what are not always needed or merit-
based.
Conflict theory involves a group in power that has the desire to stay there. Wealth and power
are tied together, with wealthy people typically being seen as the people in charge. This makes
sense in terms of government, corporations, and individuals who hold a disproportionate
amount of wealth compared to the rest of the population. [Word Count: 425]

theory-7561321

Conflict over valued opportunities may persist even when institutions publicly praise
cooperation.
Some people may still succeed on merit even in a society shaped by structural competition.

Once social roles are efficiently distributed, conflict theory would treat competition as
largely avoidable.

People in power may influence outcomes in ways that weaken a purely merit-based account
of success.

developed and changed over time, how it relates to other sociological theories, and whether or
not it's still relevant to life today. Even though the term might sound a little complex, conflict
theory is a straightforward idea and it can be used to explain numerous elements of our lives,
such as social classes and wealth inequality. People often think of this theory in terms of why
war and other major conflicts take place, but we can also think about it in our everyday lives.
Conflict theory is based on a few principles: That we have a limited amount of resources in our
world, that humans operate out of self-interest, and that conflict can't be avoided within and
between social groups. It's considered the opposite of an idea called functionalism, which
claims that society will naturally work together for the greater good and every individual
serves a function towards that. This theory is taught in sociology courses, and its principles
since Marx presented them have been broadened over the years to include explanations for
war and racial inequality. The idea that we all have to compete is central to conflict theory. We
see this play out, in ways such as "people competing for a limited number of jobs that pay well
and have good benefits, or for a limited supply of affordable housing in a desirable area." In
this competition, who performs a function best does not innately lead them to achieve success.
These issues arise from there not being enough of these necessities to accommodate everyone
in society and we know that decisions about who gets what are not always needed or merit-
based.
Conflict theory involves a group in power that has the desire to stay there. Wealth and power
are tied together, with wealthy people typically being seen as the people in charge. This makes
sense in terms of government, corporations, and individuals who hold a disproportionate
amount of wealth compared to the rest of the population. [Word Count: 425]

Oil prices, which briefly cooled to $95 after spiking close to $120, are poised to climb again.
Ripple effects are unmistakable — fertilisers, polymers, and a wide range of downstream
industries, remain under sustained pressure. In such a fragile moment, the prospect of
renewed hostilities is not just undesirable; it is untenable. Perhaps expectations of a swift
resolution were misplaced from the outset. The scale of devastation inflicted during the conflict
runs deep. Coordinated US-Israel strikes significantly weakened Iran’s political and military
command structures, while also leaving civilian infra scarred. Tehran’s retaliatory targeting of
Gulf Arab states, meanwhile, marked a dangerous escalation, breaching long-standing red
lines and intensifying mistrust. The animosity is real, layered, and far from easily resolved.
And yet, amid the bleakness, there is a sliver of cautious optimism. The very fact that both
sides agreed to sit across the table marks a notable shift.
This was their first direct engagement in a decade, and the highest-level dialogue since the
Tranian Revolution. Diplomacy often begins not with agreement, but with willingness — and
that, at least, has re-emerged. Still, the distance between positions remains vast. Iran seeks
sweeping concessions: control over Strait of Hormuz, war reparations, and a region-wide
ceasefire. Washington, by contrast, remains singularly focused on curbing Iran’s nuclear
ambitions and ensuring the reopening of Hormuz. Hovering over these demands is a profound
deficit of trust. US withdrawal from the Iran nuclear deal in 2018 continues to cast a long
shadow, as does Iran’s subsequent acceleration of uranium enrichment.
Complicating matters further is Iran’s past use of diplomatic breathing room to expand its
regional influence through groups like Hezbollah. Yet, abandoning dialogue now would be a
grave miscalculation. The economic toll alone demands restraint: US inflation has surged
sharply, while Iran faces a collapsing currency and staggering food inflation. What is urgently

needed are off-ramps — pragmatic pathways to de-escalation. A potential opening may lie in
upcoming Lebanon-Israel talks, which could end up cutting out Hezbollah, and offer all sides a
face-saving exit. For now, the immediate priority is clear: extend the fragile ceasefire, resist
the pull of escalation, and give diplomacy the time it, so desperately, requires. [Word Count:
431]

XVII. Do you know that Nature has its own glow at night? If you switch off all the lights at night and
walk in the garden, you might just see tiny flashes of light from insects called fireflies! Many
animals, especially those in the deep ocean, can create their own light to attract prey or a mate,
defend themselves or for camouflage. This is called bioluminescence. Most animals that display
bioluminescence rely on the dance of two unique chemicals. Luciferase, an enzyme, enables
luciferin to react with oxygen and release energy in the form of light. About 76% of all marine
animals are bioluminescent but not freshwater animals. Only the freshwater snail (Latia
neritoides) found in the streams of New Zealand releases a glowing slime when bothered.
In September, the beaches of Goa or Maharashtra offer a spectacular show by marine
microorganisms called dinoflagellates. Millions of dinoflagellates create a beautiful shimmery effect

when the ocean water moves and strikes the rocks and sandy beach at night. Movement stimulates
them, so if you run your hand in the water, it will look like it’s glowing!
Some animals like the angler fish and squid do not use luciferase and luciferin. Instead, they grow
bioluminescent bacteria in special organs. In this symbiotic relationship, the bacteria provide light
while the marine animal provides them nutrition and protection. Bioluminescence is a “cold light”,
which means that the light generated does not produce heat. Some insects, such as the larvae of the
railroad worm, a North American beetle, display a multicoloured glow. The head glows red and its
body glows green; just like a traffic signal. The vampire squid has a peculiar defence mechanism.
When threatened, it squirts a cloud of glowing mucus into its attacker’s face and then swims away!
In the dense forests of the Western Ghats, a type of fungi called Mycena lights up the forest floor
and tree trunks with what is called “foxfire”. It is thought that these fungi glow to attract insects to
spread their spores or to warn away predators. During World War I, soldiers used glow worms to
read important messages or maps in the dark without giving their position away. Today, a new
phenomenon called “light pollution” is disrupting Nature’s glow. With the development of LED,
solar, and bright street lights, our nights are getting brighter. Most animals that produce
bioluminescence rely on the cycle of day and night and do not display bioluminescence without
complete darkness. [Word Count: 409]

content.passageText:
XVII. Do you know that Nature has its own glow at night? If you switch off all the lights at night and
walk in the garden, you might just see tiny flashes of light from insects called fireflies! Many
animals, especially those in the deep ocean, can create their own light to attract prey or a mate,
defend themselves or for camouflage. This is called bioluminescence. Most animals that display
bioluminescence rely on the dance of two unique chemicals. Luciferase, an enzyme, enables
luciferin to react with oxygen and release energy in the form of light. About 76% of all marine
animals are bioluminescent but not freshwater animals. Only the freshwater snail (Latia
neritoides) found in the streams of New Zealand releases a glowing slime when bothered.
In September, the beaches of Goa or Maharashtra offer a spectacular show by marine
microorganisms called dinoflagellates. Millions of dinoflagellates create a beautiful shimmery effect

when the ocean water moves and strikes the rocks and sandy beach at night. Movement stimulates
them, so if you run your hand in the water, it will look like it’s glowing!
Some animals like the angler fish and squid do not use luciferase and luciferin. Instead, they grow
bioluminescent bacteria in special organs. In this symbiotic relationship, the bacteria provide light
while the marine animal provides them nutrition and protection. Bioluminescence is a “cold light”,
which means that the light generated does not produce heat. Some insects, such as the larvae of the
railroad worm, a North American beetle, display a multicoloured glow. The head glows red and its
body glows green; just like a traffic signal. The vampire squid has a peculiar defence mechanism.
When threatened, it squirts a cloud of glowing mucus into its attacker’s face and then swims away!
In the dense forests of the Western Ghats, a type of fungi called Mycena lights up the forest floor
and tree trunks with what is called “foxfire”. It is thought that these fungi glow to attract insects to
spread their spores or to warn away predators. During World War I, soldiers used glow worms to
read important messages or maps in the dark without giving their position away. Today, a new
phenomenon called “light pollution” is disrupting Nature’s glow. With the development of LED,
solar, and bright street lights, our nights are getting brighter. Most animals that produce
bioluminescence rely on the cycle of day and night and do not display bioluminescence without
complete darkness. [Word Count: 409]

XVIII. Relationship Note for this puzzle. Use the following standard meanings:
e First cousins share the same grandparents.
e Second cousins share the same great-grandparents.
e First cousin once removed means a one-generation gap from a first-cousin relationship.
e Second cousin once removed means a one-generation gap from a second-cousin relationship.
e Third cousins share the same great-great-grandparents.
At the annual Sharma Legacy Lunch, eight relatives sat around a circular table, all facing the
centre.
The eight people were Ishan, Juhi, Karan, Lavya, Manav, Ovi, Pranav, and Rhea.
The family background was as follows:
Jagat and Leela were the common ancestors of the branch gathered here.
They had two children: Mahesh and Nitin.
Mahesh had three children: two daughters, Asha and Charu, and one son, Bharat.
Asha had two children: one son, Ishan, and one daughter, Juhi.
Bharat had two children: one son, Karan, and one daughter, Lavya.
Charu had one son: Manav.
Nitin had one daughter: Nisha.
Nisha had two children: one daughter, Ovi, and one son, Pranav.
Ovi had one daughter: Rhea.
Thus:
Ishan, Juhi, Karan, Lavya, and Manav are first cousins.
Ovi and Pranav are second cousins of Ishan, Juhi, Karan, Lavya, and Manav.
Rhea is second cousin once removed to Ishan, Juhi, Karan, Lavya, and Manav.
The seating clues are as follows:
e Jshan sat immediately counterclockwise of one of his second cousins.
e Ishan was not adjacent to either child of Bharat.
e Ishan’s two second cousins from the same generation sat opposite each other.
e Manav sat immediately counterclockwise of Juhi.
e Juhi sat immediately counterclockwise of Ishan.www.lawpreptutorial.com
e Rhea, the only second cousin once removed at the table, sat between Bharat’s two children.
e Of Bharat’s two children, the daughter sat immediately clockwise of Rhea.
After the lunch, the organiser argued that the seating had worked particularly well because, on the
whole, closer blood relatives had been placed nearer one another, which made conversation easier
and more animated. He therefore suggested using the same principle at the next reunion.
A family counsellor disagreed. She argued that one successful lunch does not prove that
genealogical closeness itself caused the lively interaction. In her view, the success might just as
easily have come from age similarity, temperament, shared interests, or the fact that several
people may have interacted more across the table than with their immediate neighbours.
The family committee plans to review observation notes and feedback cards before deciding
whether the same seating principle should be used again.
content.questionText: Who sits second clockwise from Ishan, and how is that person related to Ishan?
options: Karan, first cousin
Rhea, second cousin once removed
Ovi, second cousin
Lavya, first cousin
content.explanation: Karan, first cousin: This is correct because Karan is indeed second clockwise from Ishan, and the relationship is also correct.

evidence.explanation: Karan, first cousin: This is correct because Karan is indeed second clockwise from Ishan, and the relationship is also correct.

SECTION I
I.	The human mind is a restless blend of past memories, future anxieties, and current desires. It
is often likened to a “monkey” jumping from thought to thought. Natural human qualities such
as desire, fear, attachment, and comparison drive this constant inner race. When desires go
unmet, or we face the loss of what we are attached to, the mind suffers.
Sri Thannerpalli Krishnan Swamy explained the spiritual concept of “Jalasandhi” — the
confluence of two rivers, or a river meeting the ocean — and compared it to a profound
metaphor for the human condition. Water never stays still and always finds a way around
obstacles. In the same way, the mind remains in a state of flux. At a confluence, separate
streams merge into one current. Ideally, our diverse experiences and emotions should become
a source of calm. Yet, humans are often distracted by bodily desires and lose sight of the
higher purpose of birth.
Continuing this exploration of the mind’s nature, controlling it is difficult due to the three
gunas (qualities) inherent in the body: Sattva (honesty and peace), Rajas (passion and anger),
and Tamas (impatience and ignorance). According to the laws of Karma, humans often
struggle with lower levels of Sattva and higher levels of Rajas and Tamas. This imbalance
leads to ahankara (false ego), where the spirit soul becomes bewildered and mistakenly
identifies itself with the perishable body.
Given these challenges, to overcome these spiritual hurdles and focus on the atma (soul), the
scriptures suggest three primary paths. First, one must cultivate Sattva guna. Second, one
should practise moderation in worldly affairs, maintaining just enough attachment to fulfil
duties while focusing on spiritual growth. Finally, one should seek “Acharya Parampara” —
the company and blessings of the great teachers. By serving those who have attained wisdom
through discipline and penance, one can alleviate one’s own obstacles and sins, leading to a
clearer, more peaceful life. [Psychology; Word Count: 315]

SECTION I
I.	The human mind is a restless blend of past memories, future anxieties, and current desires. It
is often likened to a “monkey” jumping from thought to thought. Natural human qualities such
as desire, fear, attachment, and comparison drive this constant inner race. When desires go
unmet, or we face the loss of what we are attached to, the mind suffers.
Sri Thannerpalli Krishnan Swamy explained the spiritual concept of “Jalasandhi” — the
confluence of two rivers, or a river meeting the ocean — and compared it to a profound
metaphor for the human condition. Water never stays still and always finds a way around
obstacles. In the same way, the mind remains in a state of flux. At a confluence, separate
streams merge into one current. Ideally, our diverse experiences and emotions should become
a source of calm. Yet, humans are often distracted by bodily desires and lose sight of the
higher purpose of birth.
Continuing this exploration of the mind’s nature, controlling it is difficult due to the three
gunas (qualities) inherent in the body: Sattva (honesty and peace), Rajas (passion and anger),
and Tamas (impatience and ignorance). According to the laws of Karma, humans often
struggle with lower levels of Sattva and higher levels of Rajas and Tamas. This imbalance
leads to ahankara (false ego), where the spirit soul becomes bewildered and mistakenly
identifies itself with the perishable body.
Given these challenges, to overcome these spiritual hurdles and focus on the atma (soul), the
scriptures suggest three primary paths. First, one must cultivate Sattva guna. Second, one
should practise moderation in worldly affairs, maintaining just enough attachment to fulfil
duties while focusing on spiritual growth. Finally, one should seek “Acharya Parampara” —
the company and blessings of the great teachers. By serving those who have attained wisdom
through discipline and penance, one can alleviate one’s own obstacles and sins, leading to a
clearer, more peaceful life. [Psychology; Word Count: 315]

I.	When Persianised Turks linked to the Delhi Sultanate extended their authority into the
Bengal delta in the early 13th century, Islamic culture gradually took root in locally
distinctive forms. This process became especially pronounced after the mid-fourteenth century,
when Bengal’s Muslim rulers cut ties with the sultans of Delhi. From 1342 until the Mughal
conquest in the early seventeenth century, a succession of independent dynasties governed the
region. During this period, Persian functioned as both the language of administration and the
medium of courtly life.
Historian Richard Eaton notes that Bengal functions as a linguistic archive of an earlier
Persian world. India becomes like a deep freeze container that preserves this much earlier

vocabulary. Words that disappeared from Persian centuries ago still survive in Bengali —
piyala (cup), no longer used in Iran, and aasta (slow), replaced today by yavash. Even common
expressions like griftar kora (to arrest) derive from Persian. This long cohabitation with the
Persian language and a courtly culture rooted in Turko-Persian traditions played a pivotal
role in shaping the middle Bengali language, literature, and culture, which eventually entered
into the complex trajectories of colonial modernity in the nineteenth century.
Although Persian was present in regions such as Sind, Multan, and Punjab before the twelfth
century, it was the Turkish conquests in northern India and the rise of the Delhi Sultanate
that enabled the language to assume a far more prominent and sustained role. Despite the
considerable cultivation of Persian in pre-Mughal India, it was undoubtedly the Mughal
imperial state which presided over the ‘most productive — perhaps even incomparable —
efflorescence of Persian literary culture’ in India.
The centrality of Persian to Mughal political culture was firmly established under Akbar who
declared it the official language of governance. Chatterjee further argues that Persian
possessed a unique capacity to function as an effective medium of governance. Sanskrit,
though prestigious and sacred, was not considered suitable for a Muslim ruling elite, while
regional vernaculars were often viewed as too limited in scope for imperial administration.
[Culture; Word Count: 334]

content.passageText:
IV.	In the early 2020s, secularization stopped: After rising for 15 years, the nonreligious share of
the American population suddenly stopped growing. Ever since, there’s been a vigorous debate
over whether this plateau is a precursor to religious revival or just a levelling off preceding a
further fall from faith.
The revivalists tend to have vivid anecdotes — Bible sales climbing, young American men
storming the doors of Eastern Orthodoxy, Catholic baptisms surging in France. The no-
revivalists tend to have deflating data. No, Gen Z isn’t more religious than the millennials. No,
evangelical churchgoing didn’t surge after Charlie Kirk’s murder. Yes, church attendance is
ticking up in some traditions, but it might just be churches regaining people who stopped
going during the pandemic.
With Easter looming, let’s throw out some recent examples of conflicting revival-related
evidence. First, new data showing that in 2025 the nonreligious share of the American
population declined yet again, with the atheist-agnostic share back down to the levels of 2014.
(A point for the revivalists!) Second, a retraction of a much-cited study in Britain that
purported to show a Christian revival among younger people in England and Wales. (A point
for the no-revivalists!) Third, a story by my colleagues tracking a big rise in conversions to
Roman Catholicism across many American dioceses. Fourth, a Pew Research Center survey
showing that Catholicism loses far more lapsed Catholics than it gains in converts.
Putting the last two Catholic trends together helps explain a key reason this debate is so
unsettled: It’s entirely possible for a faith to experience revival and decline simultaneously.
That’s because conversion is a different thing, sociologically and personally, than what you
might call the ordinary transmission of an established faith. Not a completely different thing,
to be sure: People can have conversion experiences inside their inherited religions, with
evangelical Christianity in particular encouraging a conversion mentality (being “saved,”
getting “born again”) among its younger adherents.
[Religion and Society; Word Count: 319]

revivalists tend to have deflating data. No, Gen Z isn’t more religious than the millennials. No,

ticking up in some traditions, but it might just be churches regaining people who stopped
going during the pandemic.

evidence. First, new data showing that in 2025 the nonreligious share of the American
population declined yet again, with the atheist-agnostic share back down to the levels of 2014.
(A point for the revivalists!) Second, a retraction of a much-cited study in Britain that
purported to show a Christian revival among younger people in England and Wales. (A point
for the no-revivalists!) Third, a story by my colleagues tracking a big rise in conversions to
Roman Catholicism across many American dioceses. Fourth, a Pew Research Center survey
showing that Catholicism loses far more lapsed Catholics than it gains in converts.

unsettled: It’s entirely possible for a faith to experience revival and decline simultaneously.

CEOs of Korean Companies.

together in concrete ways in multiple domains to bring lasting prosperity, peace and progress
to their peoples and to foster meaningful cooperation among them in a turbulent and fast-

changing world. They announced the following Joint Strategic Vision for implementing and
adding further content to the India-ROK Special Strategic Partnership. India and the ROK,
two vibrant and resilient democracies of Asia and leading world economies, are connected by
deep historical ties and mutual goodwill between their peoples. India and the ROK also
acknowledge the significant role of their partnership in fostering peace, stability, and security
in the Indo-Pacific region. Taking note of the visit of the ROK Deputy Speaker to India, the
two leaders supported regular exchanges of Speakers and Members of the Parliament of India
and the National Assembly of the ROK. To bring the next generation of thought leaders of
India and the ROK closer, the two leaders welcomed the launch of respective programmes and
initiatives by the two Foreign Ministries. [Word Count: 250]

in 2028, according to the latest data released on May 6, by the National Crime Records Bureau
(NCRB). The crime rate, measured in terms of cases registered per lakh population, dipped
correspondingly from 448.3 in 2023 to 418.9 in 2024. Of the recorded cases, 35.44 lakh were
registered under the Indian Penal Code (IPC) and the Bharatiya Nyay Sanhita (BNS), and
23.41 lakh under special and local laws, the report revealed.
This apparent improvement in the overall crime figures ought to be analysed keeping in mind
the complicated reality, with cybercrime, crimes against children and economic offences posing
significant concerns, and the potential impact of legislative reclassification on reflected
numbers.

major 30.58% drop, reducing from 6.36 lakh to 4.41 lakh in 2024. NCRB, however, clarified
that the dip in cases under ‘hurt or grievous hurt' may be attributed to changes in the BNS,
which replaced the IPC in 2023. Sections of 'hurt or grievous hurt' have been merged while
‘simple hurt' has been reclassified as a non-cognisable offence, meaning it no longer appears in
police registration data. Thus, the fall is likely attributed to legislative change rather than an
actual reduction in number of incidents. [Word Count: 226]

VIII. India is learnt to be no longer inclined in hosting the COP33 climate meeting in 2028. India
had not formally bid for the event, but Prime Minister Narendra Modi had made the offer in
December 2023, during the COP28 meeting in Dubai. These meetings decide the global course
of action on climate change. COP, or Conference of Parties, is the annual meeting of the
signatories to the 1994 UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC). It also
serves as the meeting of the signatories to the 2015 Paris Agreement, and 1997 Kyoto
Protocol. Despite the fact that a COP33 cell had been set up under the Climate Change
division in the Ministry of Environment, Forests and Climate Change last year to prepare the
country for hosting the event.

There was a growing realisation within the government that as the host and President of the
conference, India would be expected to champion and prioritise the global cause on climate
change which could sometimes come in conflict with its own national positions on many
climate-related issues. COP33 is due to carry out a Global Stocktake (GST) of climate actions
to assess how the world has progressed on the Paris Agreement target of keeping global rise in
temperatures within 1.5 or 2 degree Celsius from pre-industrial times. Countries are expected
to raise the ambition of their climate action based on this exercise. There is greater scrutiny on
the climate actions of the host country which is supposed to act as the global climate leader
during its presidency. Besides, global events in the last few years, on the climate front and
elsewhere, had substantially altered the climate negotiation landscape, with divisions between
countries on several issues getting sharpened. India itself has been taking strong positions on
some of these issues.
