SECTION III
X.	The Uniform Civil Code means one country one rule in matters of personal law. Civil Code
covers laws governing personal matters such as marriage, divorce, maintenance, adoption,
inheritance, succession and guardianship. Article 44 of the Constitution declares that the
State shall endeavour to secure for citizens a Uniform Civil Code throughout the territory of
India. However, Article 44 is placed under the Directive Principles of State Policy and is not
enforceable by courts. The idea is to combine different personal laws into one common law
applicable to all citizens irrespective of religion, race, caste or community. At the same time, it
has been opposed on the ground that it may affect religious freedom under Articles 25 and 26.
India is a secular and diverse country where Hindus, Muslims, Christians, Parsis and other
communities are governed by separate personal laws. Hindus are governed by laws such as
the Hindu Marriage Act, Hindu Succession Act, Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act and
Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, while Muslims are governed by the Shariat
Application Act, Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act and other personal law principles. This
lack of uniformity creates difficulties in matters of succession, divorce, inheritance, adoption
and maintenance, and makes it difficult for judges to apply one common standard of justice.
The Uniform Civil Code was debated in the Constituent Assembly. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, K.M.
Munshi, Alladi Krishnaswamy Ayyar and others supported it as a step towards national unity,
secularism and social reform. However, due to strong opposition, especially from members
concerned about interference with Muslim personal law, it was placed only as a Directive
Principle. Supporters argued that religion should be separated from social relations and that
personal laws should not obstruct equality.
Uniform Civil Code is also closely linked with gender justice. Personal laws of different
communities have often placed women in an inferior position in matters of marriage, divorce,
maintenance and inheritance. Problems such as polygamy, desertion, cruelty and triple talaq
show how women may suffer under unequal personal laws. A common civil law can help
promote equality between men and women and reduce discrimination.
Goa is often cited as an example because it follows a uniform family law applicable to all
communities. The judiciary has also repeatedly discussed the need for UCC in cases such as
Shah Bano, Sarla Mudgal, Narasu Appa Mali and Lily Thomas. The Supreme Court has
supported the desirability of UCC, while also recognising that social acceptance and legislative
will are necessary for its implementation. [Constitutional Law-UNIFORM CIVIL CODE; Word
Count: 413]
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from, htips://thelawwaywithlawyers.com/uniform-
civil-code-in-india-a-constitutional-mandateoraculturalconundrum/

SECTION III
X.	The Uniform Civil Code means one country one rule in matters of personal law. Civil Code
covers laws governing personal matters such as marriage, divorce, maintenance, adoption,
inheritance, succession and guardianship. Article 44 of the Constitution declares that the
State shall endeavour to secure for citizens a Uniform Civil Code throughout the territory of
India. However, Article 44 is placed under the Directive Principles of State Policy and is not
enforceable by courts. The idea is to combine different personal laws into one common law
applicable to all citizens irrespective of religion, race, caste or community. At the same time, it
has been opposed on the ground that it may affect religious freedom under Articles 25 and 26.
India is a secular and diverse country where Hindus, Muslims, Christians, Parsis and other
communities are governed by separate personal laws. Hindus are governed by laws such as
the Hindu Marriage Act, Hindu Succession Act, Hindu Adoption and Maintenance Act and
Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, while Muslims are governed by the Shariat
Application Act, Dissolution of Muslim Marriages Act and other personal law principles. This
lack of uniformity creates difficulties in matters of succession, divorce, inheritance, adoption
and maintenance, and makes it difficult for judges to apply one common standard of justice.
The Uniform Civil Code was debated in the Constituent Assembly. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, K.M.
Munshi, Alladi Krishnaswamy Ayyar and others supported it as a step towards national unity,
secularism and social reform. However, due to strong opposition, especially from members
concerned about interference with Muslim personal law, it was placed only as a Directive
Principle. Supporters argued that religion should be separated from social relations and that
personal laws should not obstruct equality.
Uniform Civil Code is also closely linked with gender justice. Personal laws of different
communities have often placed women in an inferior position in matters of marriage, divorce,
maintenance and inheritance. Problems such as polygamy, desertion, cruelty and triple talaq
show how women may suffer under unequal personal laws. A common civil law can help
promote equality between men and women and reduce discrimination.
Goa is often cited as an example because it follows a uniform family law applicable to all
communities. The judiciary has also repeatedly discussed the need for UCC in cases such as
Shah Bano, Sarla Mudgal, Narasu Appa Mali and Lily Thomas. The Supreme Court has
supported the desirability of UCC, while also recognising that social acceptance and legislative
will are necessary for its implementation. [Constitutional Law-UNIFORM CIVIL CODE; Word
Count: 413]

XI.	Homicide means killing of one human being by another human being. The word comes from
Latin terms “homo”, meaning man, and “cida”, meaning to kill. However, all homicide does not
amount to murder. Section 100 of the BNS deals with culpable homicide, which includes acts
causing death but not necessarily amounting to murder. Murder is also a form of homicide, but
it is graver, more intensive, and is punished more severely. Section 101 of BNS defines murder
and explains when culpable homicide becomes murder.
The main difference between culpable homicide and murder is based on intention, knowledge,
and the degree of certainty of death. If the person committing the act has complete knowledge
that the act will, in all probability, cause death, and still deliberately commits it with free will
and intention, the act amounts to murder. In culpable homicide not amounting to murder,
there may be intention to cause death or bodily injury, but there is no certainty that death will
necessarily follow. Section 100 of BNS uses the expression “likely to cause death,” while
Section 101 of BNS uses stronger expressions such as “sufficient in the ordinary course of
nature to cause death” and “so imminently dangerous that it must, in all probability, cause
death.” www.lawpreptutorial.com
The difference can be understood through examples. If Z hates X and merely prays for X’s
death, no offence is committed because prayer does not cause death. If Z pushes X into an
eight-foot pit and X dies, it may amount to culpable homicide if Z did not know that death was
certain. But if Z ensures that X receives no food, water, or air until death, it becomes murder
because death is the natural and certain consequence.
In Nara Singh Challan v. State of Orissa, the court held that Section 100 is the genus and
Section 101 is the species. In Reg v. Govinda, the accused struck his wife and placed his foot
on her chest, resulting in death, but the act was treated as culpable homicide not amounting to
murder because death was not necessarily likely in the ordinary course. In State of A.P. v. R.
Punnayya, the Supreme Court explained three degrees of culpable homicide: murder under
Section 300, culpable homicide under Section 304 Part I, and the least grave form under
Section 304 Part II.
Confusion arises because intention and knowledge are difficult to prove. Courts examine facts,
pre-planning, grave provocation, sudden fight, fear, or private defence. Cases such as Ram
Kumar v. State of Chhattisgarh, Bhagwan Singh v. State of Uttarakhand, and Macchi Singh
v. State of Rajasthan show how courts decide punishment based on the gravity, knowledge,
intention, brutality, and surrounding circumstances. [Criminal Law-Culpable Homicide and
Murder under BNS; Word Count: 443]

and testamentary succession and to create clarity in situations where property devolves after
death. It mainly applies to Christians, Parsis, and persons governed by the Special Marriage
Act in certain cases. It generally does not apply to Hindus, Muslims, Buddhists, Sikhs, and
Jainas, except where specifically provided, as seen from provisions such as Sections 4, 29 and
58. Section 2 defines important terms such as will, executor, administrator, codicil and
probate. A will is the legal declaration of the intention of a testator regarding distribution of
property after death, while probate is a certified copy of a will granted by a competent court.
Domicile under Sections 4 to 19 plays a critical role in determining which law governs
succession, especially where property is located across different jurisdictions. Section 5
provides that succession to immovable property in India is governed by Indian law, while
succession to movable property is governed by the law of the domicile of the deceased. The Act
recognises domicile of origin, domicile of choice and declared domicile. It also states that a
person can have only one domicile, the domicile of origin continues until a new one is acquired,
a minor’s domicile follows that of the parent, and a married woman acquires the domicile of
her husband. Sections 20 to 22 further clarify that marriage does not automatically create
proprietary interest in the property of a spouse.
The Act also provides rules on consanguinity and kindred under Sections 23 to 28.
Consanguinity means relationship between persons descended from a common ancestor and
may be lineal or collateral. There is no distinction between paternal and maternal relations or
full blood and half blood, and posthumous children are included. Intestate succession under
Sections 29 to 49 applies where a person dies without a valid will. Property generally devolves
upon the spouse, lineal descendants and kindred. A widow gets one-third where lineal
descendants exist, one-half where only kindred exist, and the whole property where no
kindred exists. A husband has the same rights in the wife’s property.
For Parsis, Sections 50 to 56 create a separate scheme where property is divided among widow
or widower, children, parents and next-of-kin. Testamentary succession deals with wills.

Under Section 59, any major person of sound mind can make a will. A will made by fraud,
coercion or undue influence is invalid under Section 61. Section 63 requires signature by the
testator and attestation by two witnesses. Privileged wills may be made by soldiers, airmen
and mariners with relaxed formalities. Probate, letters of administration and succession
certificates under later provisions regulate estate administration and recovery of debts and
securities.

XIV. The 1956 Articles concerning the Law of the Sea were adopted by the International Law
Commission at its eighth session and submitted to the General Assembly as part of the
Commission’s report. The Commission considered that the law of the sea involved legal,
technical, biological, economic and political aspects, and recommended an international
conference to embody the results in conventions or other appropriate instruments. The draft
applies to the law of the sea in time of peace only, and the term “mile” means a nautical mile
of 1,852 metres. www.lawpreptutorial.com
The draft begins with the territorial sea. It states that the sovereignty of a State extends toa
belt of sea adjacent to its coast, called the territorial sea, and also extends to the air space over
it, its bed and subsoil. The Commission recognised that State practice on the breadth of
territorial sea was not uniform, but considered that international law did not permit extension
beyond twelve miles. The breadth was to be measured from the low-water line, subject to
special rules on straight baselines, bays, ports, roadsteads, islands, drying rocks, opposite
coasts, adjacent States and river mouths.

The Articles also recognise the right of innocent passage. Ships of all States may pass through
the territorial sea, but passage remains innocent only when the ship does not commit acts
prejudicial to the security of the coastal State or contrary to international law. Foreign ships
must comply with the coastal State’s transport and navigation laws. No charge may be levied
merely for passage, except for specific services rendered. The coastal State’s criminal and civil
jurisdiction over foreign ships during passage is limited, and warships may be required to give
prior authorisation or notification.
For the high seas, the draft defines them as all parts of the sea not included in the territorial
sea or internal waters. No State may validly subject any part of the high seas to its
sovereignty. Freedoms of the high seas include navigation, fishing, laying submarine cables
and pipelines, and overflight. Ships sail under the flag of one State only, and there must be a
genuine link between the ship and the flag State. The draft further deals with warship
immunity, safety of navigation, duty to render assistance, prevention of slave trade, repression
of piracy, right of visit, hot pursuit, conservation of living resources, submarine cables and
pipelines, contiguous zone control, and continental shelf rights for exploration and exploitation
of natural resources.
[International Law-United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS); Word
Count:405]
Source: Extracted with edits and revisions from,
hittps://legal.un.org/ilc/texts /instruments/english/draft_articles/8_1_8 2_1956.pdf

XIV. The 1956 Articles concerning the Law of the Sea were adopted by the International Law
Commission at its eighth session and submitted to the General Assembly as part of the
Commission’s report. The Commission considered that the law of the sea involved legal,
technical, biological, economic and political aspects, and recommended an international
conference to embody the results in conventions or other appropriate instruments. The draft
applies to the law of the sea in time of peace only, and the term “mile” means a nautical mile
of 1,852 metres. www.lawpreptutorial.com
The draft begins with the territorial sea. It states that the sovereignty of a State extends toa
belt of sea adjacent to its coast, called the territorial sea, and also extends to the air space over
it, its bed and subsoil. The Commission recognised that State practice on the breadth of
territorial sea was not uniform, but considered that international law did not permit extension
beyond twelve miles. The breadth was to be measured from the low-water line, subject to
special rules on straight baselines, bays, ports, roadsteads, islands, drying rocks, opposite
coasts, adjacent States and river mouths.

The Articles also recognise the right of innocent passage. Ships of all States may pass through
the territorial sea, but passage remains innocent only when the ship does not commit acts
prejudicial to the security of the coastal State or contrary to international law. Foreign ships
must comply with the coastal State’s transport and navigation laws. No charge may be levied
merely for passage, except for specific services rendered. The coastal State’s criminal and civil
jurisdiction over foreign ships during passage is limited, and warships may be required to give
prior authorisation or notification.

sea or internal waters. No State may validly subject any part of the high seas to its

and pipelines, and overflight. Ships sail under the flag of one State only, and there must be a
genuine link between the ship and the flag State. The draft further deals with warship
immunity, safety of navigation, duty to render assistance, prevention of slave trade, repression
of piracy, right of visit, hot pursuit, conservation of living resources, submarine cables and

of natural resources.

XVI. The Supreme Court held that survivors of acid attacks, who were forced to consume acid and
suffered internal injuries without any visible scarring, will be considered acid attack victims
under the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (RPwD) Act, 2016. The bench of CJI Surya Kant
and Joymalya Bagchi said that the clarification would apply retrospectively from the day the
Act came into force and also informed the government that existing punishment for acid
attack had failed as a deterrent, suggested reversing the burden of proof onto the accused and
said acid sellers should be made co-accused in such cases. The order came in a petition filed by
Shaheen Malik, who herself was a survivor and had flagged a gap in law that was leaving out
an entire category of victims without access to state support.
The RPwD Act includes acid attack survivors in its list of specified disabilities. But the
definition it settled on was narrow. Under Schedule 2(zc) of the Act, an “acid attack victim” is
a person “disfigured due to violent assaults by throwing of acid or similar corrosive substance.”
Survivors who had acid forcefully ingested fell outside it. The court noted the problem was
that “the use of the term “disfigured” appears to confine the scope of external disfigurement of
the body, thereby excluding cases involving internal injuries or scarring caused by the
administration of acid.”
The injuries in such cases are equally severe. When acid is ingested, it burns the mouth,
throat, oesophagus, and stomach. The damage is quite often permanent. Malik’s petition
states that “the corrosive substance causes intense burns and significant harm to the internal
organs, particularly the gastrointestinal system. This often results in lifelong medical
complications, including the need for ongoing gastroenterological care. Victims of oral acid
ingestion may experience long-term issues such as difficulty eating, swallowing, and
digestion.”
The consequences of falling outside the purview of the RPwD Act are significant. A disability
certificate under the Act is the gateway to financial assistance, rehabilitation schemes,
medical support, etc. Without it, a survivor cannot access any of it. The petition called it a
“textbook example of under-classification, where a law purports to treat a class of persons but
arbitrarily excludes a sub-group that is identically situated for the purposes of the law.” The
only difference between the two groups, it argued, is the method of the attack—throwing vs
administering acid, rather than the nature and extent of harm. /Law; Word Count: 406]

XVII. When spring rolls around in the northern hemisphere, so do conversations about “No Mow
May.” Homeowners forgo mowing, allowing otherwise hidden flowers to bloom in your lawn,
increasing your yard’s biodiversity and providing food for pollinator concerns like these, No
Mow May ors like bees. However, scientists have increasingly questioned whether this trend,
which began in the United Kingdom, is compatible with United States lawns. Many U.S.
lawns are filled with non-native species like dandelions (Taraxacum officinale), which
Europeans colonists introduced to North America. These plants are not necessarily a good food
source for native pollinators as they lack certain important amino acids that make nectar and
pollen nutritious. Because of concerns like these, No Mow May has actually “become quite
controversial” in the U.S. I mean, who knew dandelions could be so controversial?
“No Mow May” started in 2018 as a campaign by the U.K. organization Plantlife. The group
originally coined the slogan to encourage local U.K. councils to manage green spaces more like
traditional hay meadows to increase biodiversity. Historically, workers who tended hay
meadows let them grow long throughout spring and most of the summer, only cutting them at
the end of summer to make hay. Plantlife picked May as the month to focus on for two main
reasons: May is the month that many U.K. grassland species start to flower (although climate
change is shifting that), and May is also when farmers traditionally removed animals from
hay meadows so they could grow. Plantlife suggested local authorities test out the hay meadow
management style with “No Mow May.”
Plantlife soon realized that the slogan was catching on with the public, and that “this could be
a really great way to engage the public about the importance of grasslands. In the U.K.,
“people’s lawns are often kind of relic grasslands,” and letting them grow can reveal native
flowers they didn’t know they had in their lawn. These flowers provide nectar and pollen for
native bees and other local pollinators that evolved alongside these plants. Plantlife chose May
for its campaign because it aligns with traditional hay meadow management, not because
there was specific scientific evidence about not mowing in May. Since the campaign started,
there has been at least one study examining its effects: In 2022, Ecological Solutions and
Evidence published a paper showing that un-mowed grassland plots in the U.K. produced
more nectar in mid-late May than mowed plots, providing more food for native pollinators. But
in the United States, the effects of No Mow May aren’t necessarily the same. /Environment;
Word Count: 423]

L	When a flavour is made from scratch, Wood goes to chef Pat Clifford, who spent 14 years in
restaurants — including some with two Michelin stars — before moving into “ambient foods”
(anything in the supermarket that isn’t chilled). Clifford’s “creative design kitchen” is clean
and clinical. Bald, tall, bespectacled and wearing one smartwatch on each wrist, Clifford has a
matter-of-fact way of speaking that brings to mind a crushed peppercorn crisp.
The chef fries some pointed peppers to demonstrate how he developed a flavour that was
released in Spain in 2022. Despite traditionally being less adventurous with crisps, Spanish
appetites have changed recently thanks to younger generations being exposed to different
crisps on their travels (and on the internet). So, Clifford collaborated with a TV chef to
recreate some traditional dishes. “I went to work with Quique Dacosta in his restaurant in
Spain. He showed me how he made this dish,” he says. The peppers are fried in charcoal-
infused oil to give them a smoky flavour. The sharpness of the pepper cuts through in the real
dish and the roasted wood-fired pepper with olive oil and garlic crisps.
PepsiCo works with local chefs to understand the nuances of different cuisines. Before Lay’s
launched in Pakistan in 2007, the team researched the country’s “culinary worldview”. “What
struck me as incredibly interesting was that in Pakistani cuisine there is an expectation that
all flavours have the right spices that go with them,” Wade says. A tomato crisp wouldn’t taste
like tomato and a cheese crisp wouldn’t taste like cheese unless paired with “the right blend of
spices”. The company is evasive over email when asked what these spices are, but there are
clues on its packets. Swiss Grilled Cheese Lay’s available in Pakistan, for example, have
peppercorns and chilli pictured on the front. Spanish Tomato Tango Lay’s in India have
pictures of chilli oil and cinnamon sticks. Even when customers crave a taste of the world,
crisps are catered to local appetites.
It turns out there is one other crucial step in the process of creating a new flavour. With a
mouth stuffed full of pepper in Clifford’s kitchen, I ask: “But how do you do it? How do you
turn this dish into a powder?” That’s when I discover that they don’t. “We partner up with
these big global flavour houses, seasoning houses,” Wood says, giving no names. When I get
home and Google “seasoning house”, all it throws up is the title of a 2013 British horror film
about an orphan who murders soldiers.

IV.	I first saw Hundreds Hall when I was ten years old. It was the summer after the war, and the
Ayreses still had most of their money then, were still big people in the district. The event was
an Empire Day féte: I stood with a line of other village children making a Boy Scout salute
while Mrs Ayres and the Colonel went past us, handing out commemorative medals;
afterwards we sat to tea with our parents at long tables on what I suppose was the south lawn.
Mrs Ayres would have been twenty-four or -five, her husband a few years older; their little
girl, Susan, would have been about six. They must have made a very handsome family, but my
memory of them is vague. I recall most vividly the house itself, which struck me as an absolute
mansion. I remember its lovely ageing details: the worn red brick, the cockled window glass,
the weathered sandstone edgings. They made it look blurred and slightly uncertain—like an
ice, I thought, just beginning to melt in the sun. There were no trips inside, of course. The
doors and French windows stood open, but each had a rope or a ribbon tied across it; the
lavatories set aside for our use were the grooms’ and the gardeners’, in the stable block. My
mother, however, still had friends among the servants, and when the tea was finished and
people were given the run of the grounds, she took me quietly into the house by a side door,
and we spent a little time with the cook and the kitchen girls. The visit impressed me terribly.
The kitchen was a basement one, reached by a cool vaulted corridor with something of the feel
of a castle dungeon. An extraordinary number of people seemed to be coming and going along
it with hampers and trays. The girls had such a mountain of crockery to wash, my mother
rolled up her sleeves to help them; and to my very great delight, as a reward for her labour I
was allowed to take my pick of the jellies and ‘shapes’ that had come back uneaten from the

designed to strengthen the security of global supply chains that support artificial intelligence
(AI) and advanced semiconductor technologies. The decision reflects growing cooperation
among like-minded nations seeking to reduce vulnerabilities in critical technology sectors and
ensure uninterrupted access to essential resources.
Pax Silica focuses on building resilient supply chains for AI by promoting collaboration in
areas such as critical minerals, energy resources, advanced manufacturing, semiconductor
production, and AI model development. As AI becomes increasingly important for economic
growth, national security, and technological innovation, participating countries aim to reduce
their dependence on unstable or concentrated sources of key materials and technologies.
The European Commission confirmed its participation through its spokesperson, highlighting
the bloc's commitment to working closely with trusted international partners on Al-related
supply chain security. The Netherlands had also joined the initiative earlier, further
strengthening European participation in the alliance.
The initiative, led by the U.S. State Department, seeks to encourage greater coordination
among partner countries to safeguard critical technologies against future disruptions. By
promoting secure and diversified supply chains, Pax Silica aims to support long-term
innovation while ensuring reliable access to the resources required for developing next-
generation AI systems.
The EU's decision to become part of Pax Silica marks another step in expanding international
cooperation on emerging technologies. As geopolitical competition and _ technological
dependence continue to shape global policy, such partnerships are expected to play an
important role in strengthening economic resilience and supporting the responsible growth of
the global AI ecosystem.

chains.

content.passageText:
VII. In February 1922, Mahatma Gandhi decided to withdraw the Non-Cooperation Movement. He
felt the movement was turning violent in many places and satyagrahis needed to be properly
trained before they would be ready for mass struggles. Within the Congress, some leaders
were by now tired of mass struggles and wanted to participate in elections to the provincial
councils that had been set up by the Government of India Act of 1919. They felt that it was
important to oppose British policies within the councils, argue for reform and also
demonstrate that these councils were not truly democratic. C. R. Das and Motilal Nehru
formed the Swaraj Party within the Congress to argue for a return to council politics. But
younger leaders like Jawaharlal Nehru and Subhas Chandra Bose pressed for more radical
mass agitation and for full independence. In such a situation of internal debate and dissension
two factors again shaped Indian politics towards the late 1920s. The first was the effect of the
worldwide economic depression. Agricultural prices began to fall from 1926 and collapsed after
1930. As the demand for agricultural goods fell and exports declined, peasants found it
difficult to sell their harvests and pay their revenue. By 1930, the countryside was in turmoil.
Against this background the new Tory government in Britain constituted a Statutory
Commission under Sir John Simon. Set up in response to the nationalist movement, the
commission was to look into the functioning of the constitutional system in India and suggest
changes. The problem was that the commission did not have a single Indian member. They
were all British.
When the Simon Commission arrived in India in 1928, it was greeted with the slogan ‘Go back
Simon’. All parties, including the Congress and the Muslim League, participated in the
demonstrations. In an effort to win them over, the viceroy, Lord Irwin, announced in October
1929, a vague offer of ‘dominion status’ for India in an unspecified future, and a Round Table
Conference to discuss a future constitution. This did not satisfy the Congress leaders.
Source: India and the Contemporary World-II, NCERT, Class X, pp. 34-35.

Government of India Act, 1935
Indian Councils Act, 1892
content.explanation: The Government of India Act, 1919 (Montagu—Chelmsford Reforms) mandated that a statutory commission would review the working of the constitutional reforms after ten years. Accordingly, the Simon Commission was appointed in 1927 under the chairmanship of Sir John Simon.

content.passageText:
X.	Effective Wednesday, every petrol pump in India will dispense petrol blended with 20%
ethanol (E20), following a government mandate announced last month. The nationwide rollout
pushes ahead even as most vehicles on the road are not built for the fuel, raising concerns over
efficiency and engine wear.
The transition marks a significant milestone in India's Ethanol Blended Petrol (EBP)
Programme, which aims to increase the use of domestically produced biofuels. Ethanol,
primarily produced from sugarcane, maize, and damaged food grains, helps lower greenhouse
gas emissions while reducing the country's dependence on imported fossil fuels. The
programme also provides an additional source of income for farmers and supports the rural
economy.
However, the rollout has also raised concerns among vehicle owners. Most vehicles
manufactured in recent years are designed to operate on E20 fuel, but older vehicles may
experience a slight reduction in fuel efficiency because ethanol contains less energy than
conventional petrol. Automobile manufacturers recommend that consumers verify whether
their vehicles are E20-compatible before regular use. Experts also advise following
manufacturer guidelines for maintenance to ensure optimum engine performance and
longevity.
Despite these challenges, the government views ethanol blending as a long-term solution for
achieving energy independence and environmental sustainability. By encouraging the use of
renewable fuels and reducing reliance on imported crude oil, the E20 initiative represents an
important step towards cleaner transportation and a more resilient energy sector while
supporting India's broader climate and economic objectives.
Source: Mint, "E20 petrol rollout: What it means for your vehicle." Published 1 April 2026.

implementation of E20 petrol with a minimum RON of 95.

ethanol (E20), following a government mandate announced last month. The nationwide rollout
pushes ahead even as most vehicles on the road are not built for the fuel, raising concerns over
efficiency and engine wear.
The transition marks a significant milestone in India's Ethanol Blended Petrol (EBP)
Programme, which aims to increase the use of domestically produced biofuels. Ethanol,
primarily produced from sugarcane, maize, and damaged food grains, helps lower greenhouse
gas emissions while reducing the country's dependence on imported fossil fuels. The
programme also provides an additional source of income for farmers and supports the rural
economy.
However, the rollout has also raised concerns among vehicle owners. Most vehicles
manufactured in recent years are designed to operate on E20 fuel, but older vehicles may
experience a slight reduction in fuel efficiency because ethanol contains less energy than
conventional petrol. Automobile manufacturers recommend that consumers verify whether
their vehicles are E20-compatible before regular use. Experts also advise following
manufacturer guidelines for maintenance to ensure optimum engine performance and
longevity.
Despite these challenges, the government views ethanol blending as a long-term solution for
achieving energy independence and environmental sustainability. By encouraging the use of
renewable fuels and reducing reliance on imported crude oil, the E20 initiative represents an
important step towards cleaner transportation and a more resilient energy sector while
supporting India's broader climate and economic objectives.
Source: Mint, "E20 petrol rollout: What it means for your vehicle." Published 1 April 2026.
Based on the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas notification on the nationwide
implementation of E20 petrol with a minimum RON of 95.

IC gave Mr. Varun only 24 hours' notice and a brief summary of allegations, withholding full
witness statements. He protested that he could not prepare an adequate defence, but the IC
proceeded and found him guilty. Mr. Varun challenges the decision. How should the validity of
the IC's decision be assessed?

It is valid only if both parties were given identically brief notice and similarly limited

disclosure of allegations, both of which were denied to Mr. Varun here.

content.questionText:
Mr. Sameer and Ms. Tara, employees of Global Tech Solutions but from different departments,
attended an employer-organised team celebration/client-networking event held off-site on a
weekend. Mr. Sameer repeatedly made unwelcome romantic advances toward Ms. Tara,
including attempts to hold her hand, despite her clear discomfort and visible efforts to avoid
him. Ms. Tara felt distressed, particularly given that she would have to continue interacting
with Mr. Sameer at work. She subsequently filed a sexual harassment complaint with the
company's IC, alleging that the behaviour created a hostile environment. Is Ms. Tara's
complaint maintainable before the IC?
options:
No, unless the event was a company-sponsored or employer-organised event, as only such
occasions would fall within the extended definition of a workplace.

Yes, if the off-site event has a sufficient workplace nexus, such as being employer-
organised, work-related, or arising out of/during employment. A purely private event may
not automatically fall within POSH.

No, because the incident took place at a purely private social event entirely unrelated to
work, which cannot be brought within the scope of the statutory workplace definition.

Yes, but only if the conduct was explicitly sexual and severe in nature, as the off-site
location becomes legally irrelevant only when the behaviour meets a heightened threshold
of severity.
content.explanation: Maintainability depends on whether the event had _ sufficient workplace/employment nexus. The passage states that the POSH Act's coverage is extensive and includes places visited by an employee arising out of or during the course of employment.

XII. Overview of the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961
Dowry must be distinguished from Stridhan. Stridhan refers to property belonging to the
woman, whereas dowry refers to property or valuable security given or agreed to be given in
connection with marriage. The practice of dowry degenerated into a coercive demand, where
the groom's family expected cash, property, and other valuables as a condition of marriage.
This transformation led to widespread harassment, domestic violence, and even dowry deaths,
ultimately prompting the Indian legislature to enact the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961. The Act
was designed to curb the menace of dowry by criminalising its giving, taking, and demanding,
thereby providing a legal shield to women against such exploitative practices.
The Act defines dowry under Section 2 as any property or valuable security given or agreed to
be given, directly or indirectly, by one party to a marriage to the other party, or by the parents
or any other person, at or before or after the marriage, in connection with the marriage. This
definition excludes dower or mahr under Muslim personal law. However, Section 3(2) of the
Act provides a limited exception. Presents given at the time of marriage to the bride or the
bridegroom without any demand having been made in that behalf do not constitute dowry,
provided such presents are entered in a list maintained in accordance with the rules made
under the Act, are of a customary nature, and their value is not excessive having regard to the
financial status of the person by whom, or on whose behalf, such presents are given. The
EC-22A, First Floor, Opp. Steel Bhawan, Shastri Circle, JODHPUR (M) 76659 44999 | www.lptedtech.com	21

LPT	Law Prep Mock Test Series
person claiming the benefit of this exception must establish that all these conditions are
satisfied."
Offences occur when dowry is exchanged, demanded, or not transferred to the bride within
three months of receipt. The Act prescribes strict punishments: under Section 3, imprisonment
of at least five years and a fine of 715,000 or the value of the dowry; Section 4 punishes dowry
demands with imprisonment of not less than six months, extendable up to two years, and fine
up to 710,000; and Section 6 separately punishes failure to transfer dowry to the woman with
imprisonment of not less than six months, extendable up to two years, or fine of %5,000 to
210,000, or both. Offences under this Act are cognizable for specified purposes, non-bailable,
and non-compoundable.www.lptedtech.com
Complaints can be filed after which the police or Dowry Prohibition Officer investigate, gather
evidence, and submit a charge sheet to the magistrate. Cognizance may be taken on the court’s
own knowledge, a police report, or a complaint by the aggrieved person, her parent/relative, or
a recognised welfare institution/organisation. The burden of proof often shifts to the accused in
cases of dowry death, particularly when a woman dies under unnatural circumstances within
seven years of marriage and there is evidence of cruelty or harassment soon before death in
connection with dowry demand. Compared to other laws, this Act focuses on prohibiting dowry
transactions, while the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita retains provisions dealing with cruelty and
dowry death. The Domestic Violence Act, 2005 also complements these laws by providing civil
remedies and protection to victims. Together, they create a strong legal framework, but
societal norms, lack of awareness, and weak enforcement continue to hinder eradication of
dowry, necessitating both legal and cultural reforms.
[Word Count: 392]
Source: Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961; Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005;
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023

Mr. Sharma, a middle-class businessman, gives a gift a brand-new Toyota Fortuner to his
daughter’s husband at the time of her marriage. He claims that the gifts were given
voluntarily out of love and to maintain family prestige, and that no demand was ever made by
the groom’s family. Does this transaction amount to dowry under the Dowry Prohibition Act,
1961?
options:
No, because the gifts were given voluntarily without any demand from the groom’s side,
and Section 3(2) protects all voluntary presents made at the time of marriage.

Yes, because a luxury car like Toyota Fortuner is excessive in value relative to Mr.
Sharma’s financial status and is not of a customary nature in the community.

No, because the absence of any demand by the groom’s family is sufficient to take the
transaction outside the definition of dowry under Section 2.

Yes, because any valuable property or cash given by the bride’s family to the groom at the
time of marriage automatically constitutes dowry irrespective of voluntariness or custom.

content.questionText:
At a traditional wedding in Udaipur, both families exchange gifts as per community customs.
The bride’s family gives the groom a gold chain, traditional attire, and some silver utensils
(total value approx. %4.5 lakh). The groom’s family gives the bride gold jewellery, clothes, and
household items (total value approx. 75 lakh) and no demand was made by either side. Later, a
complaint is filed alleging that dowry was given and taken. How should this situation be
assessed?
options:
It amounts to dowry because any exchange of valuable gifts at the time of marriage falls
within the prohibition under Section 2 of the Act.

It does not amount to dowry because the gifts satisfy all the conditions of the exception
under Section 3(2), they were given without demand, are customary in nature, not
excessive in value, and were entered in lists.

It amounts to dowry because the total value of gifts exchanged exceeds %5 lakh, which
creates a presumption of dowry under the Act.

It does not amount to dowry only because the gifts were exchanged mutually; mutuality
alone is sufficient to exclude the transaction from the definition of dowry.
content.explanation: The passage clearly states that presents given at the time of marriage without demand are protected under Section 3(2) if they are customary, not excessive having regard to the financial status of the giver, and entered in a list. In this case, all conditions are satisfied.

content.questionText:
Six months after marriage, a bride dies under unnatural circumstances in her matrimonial
home. Investigations reveal that shortly before her death she was subjected to harassment and
dowry demands by her husband and in-laws. A case under Section 304B of the Bharatiya
Nyaya Sanhita (Dowry Death) is registered. In this situation, what would be the next legal
step regarding the burden of proof?
options:
The prosecution must independently prove beyond reasonable doubt that the death was
directly caused by the accused through harassment and dowry demands, as no
presumption operates in favour of the State.

Once foundational facts are shown, especially cruelty or harassment soon before death in
connection with dowry demand, the court may draw the statutory presumption, which the
accused may rebut.

The accused must prove the actual cause of death and present a defence to rebut the legal
presumption that arises against them on account of the circumstances of the death.

It would be entirely at the court's discretion to determine whether to rely on evidence
presented by the prosecution or the defence first, based on the facts of the case.
content.explanation: The passage states that the burden of proof often shifts to the accused in cases of dowry death when a woman dies under unnatural circumstances within seven years of marriage and there is evidence of cruelty or harassment soon before death in connection with dowry demand. Option B correctly captures the statutory presumption and that it is rebuttable once foundational facts are proved.

content.questionText:
The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 complements the Dowry
Prohibition Act by providing civil remedies to women facing domestic violence, including
dowry-related harassment. As noted in the passage, such civil remedies include protection
orders, residence orders, monetary relief, and compensation to address the harm suffered.
Which of the following is an order that a court could never pass under the PWDVA, given its
nature as a civil remedy statute?
options:
An order directing the respondent to cease all communication with and harassment of the
aggrieved woman, enforceable as a protection order under the statute.

An order granting the aggrieved woman the right to continue residing in the shared
household, regardless of whether she holds any ownership title over the property.

An order sentencing the respondent to three years of imprisonment as a primary remedy
for dowry-related harassment under the civil provisions of the PWDVA.

An order awarding financial compensation to the aggrieved woman for the mental torture
and emotional distress caused by domestic violence and dowry-related harassment.
content.explanation: The passage explicitly characterises the PWDVA as a statute providing civil remedies — protection orders, residence orders, monetary relief, and compensation. A criminal sentence of imprisonment is not a civil remedy and falls entirely outside the scope of what a civil remedy statute can order.

A criminal sentence of imprisonment is not a civil remedy and falls entirely outside the scope of what a civil remedy statute can order.

Dowry must be distinguished from Stridhan. Stridhan refers to property belonging to the
woman, whereas dowry refers to property or valuable security given or agreed to be given in
connection with marriage. The practice of dowry degenerated into a coercive demand, where
the groom's family expected cash, property, and other valuables as a condition of marriage.
This transformation led to widespread harassment, domestic violence, and even dowry deaths,
ultimately prompting the Indian legislature to enact the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961. The Act
was designed to curb the menace of dowry by criminalising its giving, taking, and demanding,
thereby providing a legal shield to women against such exploitative practices.
The Act defines dowry under Section 2 as any property or valuable security given or agreed to
be given, directly or indirectly, by one party to a marriage to the other party, or by the parents
or any other person, at or before or after the marriage, in connection with the marriage. This
definition excludes dower or mahr under Muslim personal law. However, Section 3(2) of the
Act provides a limited exception. Presents given at the time of marriage to the bride or the
bridegroom without any demand having been made in that behalf do not constitute dowry,
provided such presents are entered in a list maintained in accordance with the rules made
under the Act, are of a customary nature, and their value is not excessive having regard to the
financial status of the person by whom, or on whose behalf, such presents are given. The

XIII. Environmental Safeguards in India: The EPA, 1986 and the EIA Framework
India's principal legislative instrument for environmental protection is the Environment
(Protection) Act, 1986 (EPA), which empowers the Central Government to take all necessary
measures for environmental quality improvement. The Act defines environmental pollution as
the presence of any solid, liquid, or gaseous substance at concentrations harmful to the
environment, and mandates that discharge of pollutants must not exceed prescribed
regulatory standards. Under the current EPA, contravention of Section 7 or Section 8 attracts
monetary penalty under Section 14A: 21 lakh to 215 lakh, with %50,000 per day for continuing
contravention. Notably, Section 19 of the EPA permits any person — not merely government
officials — to file a complaint before a court regarding violations after giving not less than 60
days’ notice to the Central Government or authorised authority.
Complementing the EPA is the Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) framework,
operationalised through the EJA Notification, 2006. EIA is a systematic process of identifying,
predicting, and mitigating the environmental effects of proposed projects before they are
undertaken. Baseline environmental data must be sufficiently representative; reliance on only
one season may distort impact prediction. EIA applicability is determined by size, capacity,
area, location, sectoral, or schedule-based thresholds, not merely investment value. Some
projects may remain outside full EIA scrutiny because of these thresholds.
The EIA process requires the project proponent to prepare an EIA report, often through
consultants. Reports are funded by project proponents themselves, creating concerns of conflict
of interest, selective reporting, and weak accountability despite the accreditation framework.
The EIA Notification mandates public consultation and appraisal by an Expert Appraisal
Committee before environmental clearance is granted. Post-clearance monitoring is essential,
but enforcement gaps, proponent-funded assessments, copy-paste reporting, and weak
accountability mechanisms have led to credibility problems in several cases. The framework
aims to balance development with environmental protection, but its effectiveness depends on
rigorous data, independent oversight, and strict adherence to procedural safeguards.

XIV. Witness Protection Scheme, 2018 and Section 398 of the Bharatiya Nagarik
Suraksha Sanhita, 2023
The Witness Protection Scheme, 2018 was introduced to address the critical gap in protecting
witnesses who face threats for deposing against powerful accused persons. Before this Scheme,
India addressed witness protection through scattered provisions such as Section 232 of the
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (which criminalises threats to witnesses), but these did not provide
physical protection, relocation, or identity change. Since policing and public order are State
subjects, consensus could not be reached on a uniform national law for many years. High-
profile cases exposed this gap and the urgent need for a structured mechanism.
The Scheme categorises threats into three levels. Category A covers threats to life of witness
or family and provides measures such as relocation, change of identity, and video conferencing
with concealed identity. Category B covers threats to reputation or property, and Category C
covers moderate threats such as harassment. A Threat Analysis Report (TAR) prepared by
senior police officials assesses the danger to a witness, following which the competent
authority may order appropriate protection measures based on the threat level. The Scheme is
curative and remedial — it addresses threats after they arise. In contrast, bail cancellation
under Section 483 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita is a preventive and supervisory
judicial remedy for breach of bail conditions. The two are complementary but not
interchangeable.

recognition in the requirement for States to notify their own schemes, ensuring a legal
framework for witness protection across India.

XIV. Witness Protection Scheme, 2018 and Section 398 of the Bharatiya Nagarik
Suraksha Sanhita, 2023
The Witness Protection Scheme, 2018 was introduced to address the critical gap in protecting
witnesses who face threats for deposing against powerful accused persons. Before this Scheme,
India addressed witness protection through scattered provisions such as Section 232 of the
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (which criminalises threats to witnesses), but these did not provide
physical protection, relocation, or identity change. Since policing and public order are State
subjects, consensus could not be reached on a uniform national law for many years. High-
profile cases exposed this gap and the urgent need for a structured mechanism.

or family and provides measures such as relocation, change of identity, and video conferencing
with concealed identity. Category B covers threats to reputation or property, and Category C
covers moderate threats such as harassment. A Threat Analysis Report (TAR) prepared by
senior police officials assesses the danger to a witness, following which the competent
authority may order appropriate protection measures based on the threat level. The Scheme is
curative and remedial — it addresses threats after they arise. In contrast, bail cancellation
under Section 483 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita is a preventive and supervisory
judicial remedy for breach of bail conditions. The two are complementary but not
interchangeable.

XV. Menstrual Health as a Fundamental Right
On 30 January 2026, the Supreme Court of India delivered a landmark judgment in Dr. Jaya
Thakur v. Government of India & Ors., recognising menstrual health as an enforceable
component of the right to life under Article 21 of the Constitution. The case originated as a
Public Interest Litigation filed under Article 32, seeking recognition of menstrual hygiene as a
fundamental right and directing the State to implement hygiene policies in schools across
India.
The Court observed that Article 21 guarantees not mere survival but a life of dignity, privacy,
and bodily autonomy. Denial of adequate menstrual hygiene management (MHM)
infrastructure was held to cause humiliation, health risks, and loss of dignity, all of which
constitute violations of Article 21. The petitioner had further argued that inadequate facilities
violate Article 14, the right to equality, and Article 21A, the right to education.
Applying the doctrine of substantive equality under Article 14, the Court held that
menstruation is a biological reality unique to women, but the absence of facilities converts this
biological fact into a structural disadvantage, resulting in unequal access to education and
gender-based exclusion. The State, therefore, is obligated to take affirmative action rather
than merely refraining from discrimination.
On Article 21A, the Court held that 'free education' must mean the removal of all real barriers
to school attendance. Absenteeism and dropout rates among adolescent girls directly linked to
menstrual hygiene gaps were cited as evidence of this violation. The judgment also extended

The judgment reflects the concept of transformative constitutionalism using the Constitution

XVI. Search, Seizure, and Attachment: CrPC and BNSS Compared
The investigation of a criminal offence involves three critical pre-trial powers: search, seizure,
and attachment. Under the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), Sections 93-103 govern
search procedures. A Magistrate may issue a search warrant where evidence is not otherwise
obtainable or where items are suspected to be stolen or used in a crime. Section 165 CrPC
permits a police officer to search without a warrant during investigation if delay would
prejudice the case. All searches must be conducted in the presence of independent witnesses
called panchas, and compliance with Section 100 CrPC requires at least two respectable
inhabitants of the locality, preparation of a panchnama, and provision of a copy of the seized
articles list to the occupant.
Regarding seizure, Section 102 CrPC empowers police to seize property suspected to be stolen
or connected to a crime, with a mandatory report to the Magistrate. Sections 451-452 CrPC
confer judicial authority to dispose of or return property during and after trial. Attachment
under Section 83 CrPC applies to property of proclaimed offenders declared under Section 82,
covering both movable and immovable property. Section 105 CrPC extends attachment to
properties linked to offences committed outside India.www.lptedtech.com
The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023, replaces CrPC with significant
modernisation. BNSS contains search-warrant/search-related provisions in Sections 96-105
and separately provides for search by police officer during investigation under Section 185,
introducing electronic records and gender-sensitive procedures for searches involving women.
Section 106 BNSS corresponds broadly to police power to seize certain property. Section 105
BNSS introduces audio-video recording of search and seizure. Section 107 BNSS deals with
attachment, forfeiture, or restoration of property derived from criminal activity. Sections 87—
88 BNSS address attachment of proclaimed offenders' property, enabling digital notice
issuance and faster recovery proceedings.
[Word Count: 268]
Source: Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023; Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 —
Chapters VII, IX, XII

The investigation of a criminal offence involves three critical pre-trial powers: search, seizure,
and attachment. Under the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), Sections 93-103 govern

prejudice the case. All searches must be conducted in the presence of independent witnesses
called panchas, and compliance with Section 100 CrPC requires at least two respectable

XVIII. Of the several issues the US and Iran must resolve during their 60-day negotiating window,
none is more consequential for international trade and the global economy than the future of
the Strait of Hormuz. President Donald Trump has said that it will reopen toll-free, while US
Secretary of State Marco Rubio, during his ongoing visit to the Gulf, declared that “no country
is allowed to charge tolls or fees on an international waterway”. Iran, however, has announced
plans to introduce a maritime fee for vessels transiting the Strait. Whether or not this
ultimately takes the form of a formal toll, the sobering reality is that the Strait of Hormuz is
unlikely to return to its pre-war status. Iran’s de facto control, and its ability to close it in
response to Israel’s actions in Lebanon and other perceived threats, mean that the world will
have to adjust to the region’s new strategic landscape. A week after the signing of the Iran-US
MoU, traffic through the Strait remains well below pre-war levels. Even if the US and Iran
have agreed to agree, a return to business-as-usual could take weeks, if not months. Not only
will shipping contracts, insurance policies and other arrangements be redrawn, tanker
operators and their crews will now have to sail with the possibility that Iran could close the
Strait again, without notice. Its adoption of inexpensive technologies, including shore-based
anti-ship missiles, drones, speedboats and mines, has made it easier to disrupt maritime
traffic while increasing the costs. There is, however, a longer-term scenario. The Strait,
through which one-fifth of the world’s energy supplies pass, might become a diminishing asset
as Gulf countries invest in alternative pipeline routes and the world accelerates the shift to

XIX. Wimbledon has long been the temple of strawberries, cream and moisturised stiff upper lips.
It's now also the temple of arbitrage. All England Lawn Tennis & Croquet Club's debentures -
5-yr bonds that guarantee prime seats - were issued at £1,16,000 (about 21.24 cr) in 2024.
Today, they're changing hands for £3,80,000 (about 24.77 cr), a return that would make even
Djokovic blush. The men's final alone can fetch £23,000 (%28.8 lakh) for a pair of seats. That's
more than the annual rent of a modest Clapham flat. Investors justify this as luxury
entertainment morphing into an asset class. New tennis rivalries like Jannik Sinner vs Carlos
Alcaraz have driven demand, while global buyers from the US, India and the Gulf treat
Wimbledon as a hedge against being seen as culturally 'simple'. All England Club, for its part,
pockets the proceeds to fund new courts and an 8,000-seat stadium. Everyone wins - except
the 'ordinary' tennis fan left queuing overnight for a chance at the outside courts. Not to come
across as a Roland Garros socialist, isn't sport meant to be watched, not securitised? Tennis
fans in this London heatwave may fancy making money before the tournament starts on
Monday. And, true, the line between passion and profiteering is thin. But crossing it may be
the only baseline fault that makes even McEnroe shout, 'You CANNOT be serious!'
Source: https://economictimes.indiatimes.com /opinion /just-in-jest /has-wimbledon-priced-
out-its-fans/articleshow/131974610.cms

XX. In an interesting turn of events, the breakaway faction of the All India Trinamool Congress
(AITMC) in the Lok Sabha announced merger with Nationalist Citizens Party of India (NCPD),
a regional party. The faction, with 20 MPs, has sought to invoke the merger exception under
the Tenth Schedule on the grounds that it has the support of two-thirds of AITMC’s legislature
party in Lok Sabha. While this may appear to be just another episode of political realignment,
it raises a deeper question about the working of the anti-defection law: Does the Tenth
Schedule permit two-thirds of a legislature party to effectively merge a political party with
another political party? The answer to this question goes to the heart of the merger exception,
a provision that was designed to safeguard genuine mergers between political parties. The
Tenth Schedule was enacted in 1985 to curb the politics of floor crossing among elected
legislators. It provides for disqualification of legislators who voluntarily give up membership of
their political party or defy its directions in the House. Yet, the law has often operated less as
a deterrent to defections and more as a framework within which they are meticulously
planned. Much of this can be attributed to the exceptions inherent in the law itself. The Tenth
Schedule never provided for an absolute prohibition on defections. Instead, the law exempted
disqualifications in cases of a “split” in a political party and “merger” of political parties. In
2004 the split exemption was omitted due to its excessive misuse while the merger exemption
continued to survive. Over the years, the merger exception has emerged as the principal route
for group defections to seek constitutional legitimacy in India. Housed within Paragraph 4 and
divided across two sub-paragraphs, the merger exception requires two conditions to be
fulfilled: first, an original political party must merge with another political party, and second,
a minimum of two-thirds of the members of the legislature party must consent to the merger.
Only when these two conditions are met, in this exact sequence, can a group of elected
legislators claim exemption from disqualification on grounds of merger. However, in practice,
the interpretation of Paragraph 4 has strayed from its original design, focusing primarily on
the second condition alone. This has led to an approach where the numerical majority of two-
thirds of the legislature party has been deemed to be sufficient condition to claim a merger,
regardless of the merger of the original political party with another party.
Source: https://southasianherald.com/tenth-schedule-and-the-merger-loophole/

SECTION I
I.	In recent years, the global conversation around productivity has undergone a marked
transformation. Once equated with relentless output and longer working hours, productivity is
now increasingly understood through the lens of sustainability, mental health, and long-term
efficiency. This shift has been accelerated by the pandemic, which blurred the boundaries between
professional and personal life, compelling organisations to reassess their expectations from
employees.
Remote work, initially perceived as a temporary compromise, has revealed both its promise and
pitfalls. While it offers flexibility and autonomy, it has also fostered burnout by dissolving
temporal limits on labour. Employees report working longer hours, not because they are compelled
to, but because the absence of physical separation makes disengagement psychologically difficult.
Consequently, productivity measured merely by hours logged has become an unreliable indicator
of actual value created.
Moreover, cognitive science has begun to challenge the myth of sustained concentration. Research
suggests that human attention functions in cycles, not as an uninterrupted stream. Attempts to
enforce constant focus often result in diminishing returns, undermining creativity and problem-
solving. Progressive organisations, recognising this, are experimenting with shorter workweeks,
asynchronous communication, and output-oriented assessments.
However, sceptics argue that such reforms risk normalising inefficiency and eroding
accountability. They contend that flexibility, if unregulated, may privilege certain employees while
disadvantaging others whose roles demand synchronous collaboration. The challenge, therefore,
lies not in abandoning productivity metrics but in refining them to reflect meaningful contribution
rather than performative busyness.
Ultimately, redefining productivity requires a cultural recalibration—one that values depth over
immediacy and outcomes over optics. Whether institutions can achieve this balance remains
uncertain, but the conversation itself signals a departure from industrial-age assumptions about
labour.

content.passageText:
I.	There are, in every workplace, two kinds of people. The first category consists of those who, either
as a function of dedication or neurotic tendencies, check every email, answer every text and
respond with an almost annoying alacrity on the office WhatsApp group. These front-benchers are,
unsurprisingly, the blue-eyed boys and girls of upper management. More often than not, though,
they are relative outliers. The majority of the bell curve has scores of unread emails, will often
have to be reminded to check their messages and will, much to the chagrin of the powers that be,
treat the job as work that ends with the workday. It is this second category that is causing a
headache for the Delhi government.
Over the last three months, the Delhi government’s IT department has been trying to nudge
bureaucrats — including at the secretary level — to read their official emails. It seems that
despite the repeated advisories and notices, officials do not regularly log in. This is a major
problem, not least because official instructions and notices are sent to the official address. (This
begs the question of whether the notice to check the official email was sent on the official email.)
Their official email is also linked to the portals of several government portals and services. If it is
not checked for three months, the officers lose access to all that it provides.
There is no easy answer to the problem that plagues the government of Delhi. Bureaucrats, like so
many people today, are inundated — on social media, personal WhatsApp groups, etc. But then, in
every workplace, there is a price to be paid for not being up to speed — a nagging boss, an
annoying HR missive. With every unread mail, the offending officer must ask herself: Is avoiding a
bit of boredom worth the hassle, really?
content.questionText: What is the primary purpose of the passage?
options:
To present a statistically grounded sociological classification of employee behaviour supported
by empirical data from government offices.

To satirically critique bureaucratic indifference toward official email communication by
contrasting two workplace archetypes.

To propose technological and administrative reforms aimed at increasing digital compliance in
the Delhi government.

To justify delayed responsiveness in government offices on the grounds of digital overload and
communication fatigue.
content.explanation: Reference Lines: “There are, in every workplace, two kinds of people.” “Tt is this second category that is causing a headache for the Delhi government.” “Ts avoiding a bit of boredom worth the hassle, really?” The passage contrasts two categories of employees and uses this contrast to critique bureaucrats who fail to check official emails. The concluding rhetorical question reinforces the criticism in a mildly satirical tone.

I.	There are, in every workplace, two kinds of people. The first category consists of those who, either
as a function of dedication or neurotic tendencies, check every email, answer every text and
respond with an almost annoying alacrity on the office WhatsApp group. These front-benchers are,
unsurprisingly, the blue-eyed boys and girls of upper management. More often than not, though,
they are relative outliers. The majority of the bell curve has scores of unread emails, will often
have to be reminded to check their messages and will, much to the chagrin of the powers that be,
treat the job as work that ends with the workday. It is this second category that is causing a
headache for the Delhi government.
Over the last three months, the Delhi government’s IT department has been trying to nudge
bureaucrats — including at the secretary level — to read their official emails. It seems that
despite the repeated advisories and notices, officials do not regularly log in. This is a major
problem, not least because official instructions and notices are sent to the official address. (This
begs the question of whether the notice to check the official email was sent on the official email.)
Their official email is also linked to the portals of several government portals and services. If it is
not checked for three months, the officers lose access to all that it provides.
There is no easy answer to the problem that plagues the government of Delhi. Bureaucrats, like so
many people today, are inundated — on social media, personal WhatsApp groups, etc. But then, in
every workplace, there is a price to be paid for not being up to speed — a nagging boss, an
annoying HR missive. With every unread mail, the offending officer must ask herself: Is avoiding a
bit of boredom worth the hassle, really?

Til. When the town of Velmora first learned of the bridge, it did not celebrate. Bridges, the elders
insisted, were instruments of impatience. For generations, the river Arven had served not merely
as a boundary but as a tutor, instructing the townspeople in the virtues of waiting. Traders timed
their journeys to its moods; children learned early that certain crossings belonged only to certain
seasons. To conquer the river with steel seemed, to many, an act bordering on insolence.
Yet the council approved the project with unusual haste. Velmora, once peripheral and self-
contained, had begun to feel the gravitational pull of distant cities. Younger merchants
complained that the ferry rendered commerce whimsical and reputations fragile. A missed
crossing could undo months of negotiation. Efficiency, they argued, was not impatience but
survival.
Construction commenced amid a silence more unsettling than protest. The engineer, a soft-spoken
outsider named Ilyen, soon became an object of wary curiosity. He neither defended nor
disparaged the bridge; he spoke instead of load distributions and tolerances, of how structures,
like arguments, fail at their weakest points. His metaphors, though polite, irritated the elders,
who suspected that calculation was merely arrogance in numerical dress.
As pylons rose from the riverbed, subtle transformations unsettled the town. The ferry operators,
once indispensable, found themselves treated with an awkward courtesy usually reserved for the
convalescent. Children, sensing history’s pivot, abandoned old games for speculation about the
traffic the bridge would invite. Even the elders grew restless, their criticisms acquiring an urgency
that belied their professed allegiance to patience.www.lawpreptutorial.com
On the morning the bridge opened, Velmora gathered without ceremony. No speeches were made.
The first crossing fell, unexpectedly, to Mara, the eldest ferrywoman, whose livelihood the bridge
had rendered obsolete. She stepped onto the span with neither defiance nor nostalgia, pausing
midway as if to consult the river one last time. Observers later disagreed about her expression:
some detected sorrow, others relief, a few something closer to amusement.
By evening, the bridge had already begun its quiet work of rearrangement. Strangers entered.
Departures multiplied. Transactions accelerated. And the river, indifferent yet altered, flowed
beneath a structure that promised permanence while whispering, to those inclined to listen, of
stresses accumulating beyond sight.

content.passageText:
IV.	By the time the notice appeared on the college board, the banyan tree had already begun to shed.
Its leaves fell with an unhurried confidence, collecting along the stone path where students paused
between lectures. Few read the announcement fully; most registered only its headline —
Redevelopment Proposal Approved.
The tree stood at the centre of the courtyard, older than any building that now framed it.
Professors referenced it absentmindedly when giving directions, as though it were a structural
necessity rather than an organism. Alumni recalled it with a proprietary fondness, attributing to
its shade friendships, epiphanies, and occasionally academic redemption. Yet its presence had long
ago dissolved into familiarity, the kind that escapes notice precisely because it endures.
The administration’s reasoning was impeccably rational. The courtyard, they explained, occupied
valuable space that could accommodate a research wing and expanded facilities. Progress
demanded optimisation; sentiment, while understandable, could not obstruct institutional growth.
The proposal included assurances: new landscaping, commemorative plaques, even a digital
archive preserving the tree’s “legacy.”
Reactions emerged in curious forms. A few students organised petitions whose urgency wavered
between examinations and internships. Others treated the news with ironic detachment,
photographing the tree with captions that rehearsed nostalgia before loss had actually occurred.
Faculty debates grew unexpectedly philosophical, drifting from budgetary constraints to
abstractions about heritage and utility.
Only the groundskeeper, Raman, seemed untouched by deliberation. For decades he had tended
the courtyard with an attentiveness bordering on ritual, sweeping its paths before dawn and
watering the tree during summers of reluctant rain. When asked about the redevelopment, he
responded with a politeness that resisted interpretation. “Institutions,” he said once, “have longer
memories than people, but shorter patience.”
The day the workers arrived, the campus adopted a strained normalcy. Lectures proceeded.
Conversations persisted. Yet attention gravitated toward the courtyard, where the machinery

waited with an air of procedural inevitability. Raman stood nearby, neither obstructing nor
assisting, his expression unreadable.
The first cut produced no dramatic spectacle — only a sound oddly disproportionate to the act, as
though something abstract had been disturbed. Students who had never consciously valued the
tree now lingered at windows. Silence accumulated, tentative yet pervasive.
In the weeks that followed, the courtyard transformed efficiently. Concrete replaced roots. Glass
replaced shade. The new wing rose with admirable speed, celebrated in newsletters and brochures.
Life resumed its rhythms, apparently undiminished. www.lawpreptutorial.com
Yet certain absences proved resistant to articulation. Directions required revision. Gatherings
dispersed more quickly under the unmediated sun. And Raman, sweeping the newly paved
expanse each morning, found little to collect except dust, which, unlike leaves, offered no evidence
of having once belonged.

options: An actively debated political symbol whose meaning shifts across groups
A quietly pervasive presence whose importance is felt more than articulated
A decorative landmark valued primarily for its aesthetic contribution
A recently elevated emblem constructed through administrative discourse

Option A — Incorrect: There is no indication of political debate or conflicting interpretations associated with the tree.

League was barred from contesting after she was sentenced to death in absentia for crimes against
humanity linked to the 2024 crackdown.

and a blank map. He steps into a region on edge, an economy under strain and a bilateral
relationship with India that carries decades of memory. His inheritance would be defined less by
campaign rhetoric and more by geography, history, and the hard constraints of statecraft. He was
sworn in as Bangladesh’s new Prime Minister today. Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla represented
India at the ceremony. He was accompanied by the Foreign Secretary and Lok Sabha Secretary-
General. The BNP’s landslide wins on February 12 ended 18 months of interim rule and returned
competitive politics to a country of roughly 170 million. But power has changed hands without
wiping away the past.www.lawpreptutorial.com
“This victory belongs to Bangladesh, belongs to democracy,” he said after his win. “It belongs to
the people who aspire to and have sacrificed for democracy.” He also set expectations carefully.
“We are about to begin our journey in a situation marked by a fragile economy left behind by the
authoritarian regime, weakened constitutional and statutory institutions, and a deteriorating law
and order situation”. That sentence forms the spine of his premiership. Sheikh Hasina’s Awami
League was barred from contesting after she was sentenced to death in absentia for crimes against
humanity linked to the 2024 crackdown.

VII. Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla is in the eye of a storm once again, with the Congress and some
other opposition parties pressing a notice for his removal from office. Although the government
has the numbers to defeat the motion, Birla, taking a moral high ground, decided he would not
attend the proceedings of the Lok Sabha until a decision was taken on the no-confidence motion.
The notice, signed by at least (A) MPs seeking Birla’s removal, accuses him of acting in a
“blatantly partisan” manner in the Lok Sabha. This is a long-simmering friction between the
Speaker and the opposition reaching a flashpoint. Birla has been accused earlier too, with
opposition members frequently criticising him for what they call his “aggressive” posture during
their protests in the House and for his alleged partiality to the BJP. This time, the opposition’s
anger centres on Birla not allowing Rahul Gandhi to speak in the Lok Sabha about a book written
by Gen. M. M. Naravane. When Gandhi was suspended, the Opposition accused Birla of openly
espousing the ruling party’s version on all controversial matters. The bad blood between
opposition members and Birla in this Winter Session has worsened after Birla suspended eight
Lok Sabha members last week, claiming he had “credible information that several members from
the Congress would create an unprecedented incident after reaching the Honourable Prime
Minister’s seat”. The Congress denied there was any such plan by its women MPs to carry out an
“unpleasant act” or physical threat near the Prime Minister’s seat. Birla went on to cite the same
reason for Prime Minister Modi’s unprecedented absence from the House to read his response to
the Motion of Thanks.
Source: https://frontline.thehindu.com /newsletter /poll-vault-anand-mishra/om-birla-no-
confidence-opposition-parliament-crisis/article70628521.ece
