VIII. The Economic Survey 2025-26 has painted a relatively rosy picture of India’s domestic growth
outlook, raising the country’s medium-term outlook from its earlier estimates. However, it has
simultaneously outlined a relatively grim outlook for the global economy, estimating a 10-20%
chance of a crisis worse than the global financial crisis of 2008 unfolding in 2026. Even its best-
case scenario is a continuation of conditions as they were in 2025, but “increasingly less secure and
more fragile” The Survey, authored by Chief Economic Advisor, tabled in Parliament by Finance
Minister Nirmala Sitharaman, went on to say that each of its three probabilistic scenarios for the
globe could pose risks to India For India, it pointed to the growth of capital, improved labour
participation, and greater efficiency in the deployment of these two factors of production as the key
drivers of a higher medium-term growth outlook. For the current financial year 2025-26. Over the
past three years, reform momentum has strengthened across several areas relevant for medium-
term growth,” the Survey said. “Manufacturing-oriented initiatives, such as the Production-Linked
Incentive (PLI) schemes, FDI liberalisation, and logistics reforms, have supported capacity
creation.” These measures, it added, were further bolstered by sustained public investment in
physical and digital infrastructure, the simplification of tax laws, and measures targeted at
MSMEs that have sought to ease credit constraints. These reforms have coincided with stronger
corporate and financial sector balance sheets, rising formalisation of employment, and continued
improvements in tax administration,” the Survey added. “Together, these developments make a
persuasive case that India’s potential growth has risen to around 7% over the medium term.” The
Survey outlined three scenarios for the world economy that could unfold in 2026. The worst of
these, the macroeconomic consequences of which “could be worse than those of the 2008 global
financial crisis”, was assigned a probability of 10-20%.
Source: https://www.thehindu.com /business/budget /economic-survey-2025-shows-india-in-
bright-light-in-an-increasingly-darker-world/article70565615.ece

enter into force after 81 governments agreed to include it in their national laws. In total, 148
countries, representing more than three-quarters of all UN member states, have signed on to
the High Seas Treaty since it was adopted in June 2023. Countries that have fully ratified the
treaty in their national laws include island nations such as Palau, Cuba and the Maldives, as well
as some of the world’s biggest economies, including China, Germany, Japan, France and Brazil.
Coming into force on Saturday, the treaty offers new protections to an area covering two-thirds of
the world’s oceans and as many as millions of different species, many of which are still
unidentified. The director of the High Seas Alliance, a nongovernmental organisation that
supports the treaty, said the agreement offers a means to protect an “extraordinary part of our
planet”. “The High Seas are full of life, from tiny plankton all the way up to the great whales that
rely on them,” she said in a statement. “We’re only just beginning to understand how important
this vast, interconnected world is for the health of our entire planet,” she said.
Source: https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/1/16/un-treaty-to-protect-extraordinary-marine-
life-due-to-come-into-force

Paving the way for the mother of all defence deals, defence minister Rajnath Singh- lead defence
acquisition council (DAC) on Thursday approved the acquisition of 114 Rafale fighter jets from
France, just 5 days ahead of the arrival of French president Emmanuel Macron in India. Though
the ministry did not provide the exact cost of 114 Rafale jets, the proposed government-to-
government deal is expected to be worth around 3.25 lakh crore, which, when signed with France’s
Dassault Aviation after final cost negotiations and the cabinet’s approval, will make it India's
biggest defence deal since independence. About 20 of the multi-role fighters will be brought in fly-
away condition and are expected to be added to the IAF fleet by 2030, while the rest will be
manufactured with Dassault-HAL collaboration in India. The DAC nod for more Rafale jets is the
government's biggest vote of confidence on the French multirole fighter, which IAF vice-chief
described just a day before as the “operation Sindoor hero” for its precision strikes on Pakistan’s
terror infrastructure and military bases. The confrontation with Pakistan saw a systematic
campaign by social media influencers, suspected to be backed by Pakistan and China, to discredit
the French aircraft amid unconfirmed reports of the loss of the French fighter jets. The IAF
currently operates 36 Rafale jets, and the Indian Navy last year placed an order for 26 of its naval
variants.
Source: https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/defence/news/defence-council-clears-procurement-of-
114-rafales-mega-contract-set-to-become-mother-of-all-defence-deals/articleshow /128276900.cms

Paving the way for the mother of all defence deals, defence minister Rajnath Singh- lead defence
acquisition council (DAC) on Thursday approved the acquisition of 114 Rafale fighter jets from
France, just 5 days ahead of the arrival of French president Emmanuel Macron in India. Though
the ministry did not provide the exact cost of 114 Rafale jets, the proposed government-to-
government deal is expected to be worth around 3.25 lakh crore, which, when signed with France’s
Dassault Aviation after final cost negotiations and the cabinet’s approval, will make it India's
biggest defence deal since independence. About 20 of the multi-role fighters will be brought in fly-
away condition and are expected to be added to the IAF fleet by 2030, while the rest will be
manufactured with Dassault-HAL collaboration in India. The DAC nod for more Rafale jets is the
government's biggest vote of confidence on the French multirole fighter, which IAF vice-chief
described just a day before as the “operation Sindoor hero” for its precision strikes on Pakistan’s
terror infrastructure and military bases. The confrontation with Pakistan saw a systematic
campaign by social media influencers, suspected to be backed by Pakistan and China, to discredit
the French aircraft amid unconfirmed reports of the loss of the French fighter jets. The IAF
currently operates 36 Rafale jets, and the Indian Navy last year placed an order for 26 of its naval
variants.

XIII. The Supreme Court, in a recent judgment, clarified the jurisdictional framework for trial of
offences under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 (D&C Act). The bench comprising Justice
Prashant Kumar Mishra and Justice Vipul M. Pancholi held that offences punishable under
Chapter IV of the Act must be tried by a Court not inferior to a Sessions Court, and cannot be
tried by a Magistrate. The case arose from an inspection conducted on July 22, 2014, at the
manufacturing premises of M/s SBS Biotech in Himachal Pradesh, where the Drug Inspector
alleged non-maintenance of records as mandated under Schedule M and Schedule U of the Drugs
and Cosmetics Rules, 1945. Schedule M prescribes good manufacturing practices and
documentation requirements, while Schedule U specifies particulars to be shown in manufacturing
records. A re-inspection on August 5, 2014, revealed discrepancies in manufacturing, testing, and
distribution records. Following sanction on September 15, 2016, a complaint was filed on February
27, 2017, alleging contraventions of Section 18(a)(vi) read with Rule 74, and Section 22(1)(cca)
read with Section 18-B, punishable under Section 27(d) and Section 28-A. The appellants
contended that mere non-maintenance of records falls under Section 18-B, punishable under
Section 28-A with a maximum sentence of one year, making the complaint barred by limitation as
it was filed more than two and a half years after inspection. They argued that Section 18 deals
with prohibition of manufacture and sale of certain drugs, not record maintenance, and therefore
Section 27(d) was inapplicable. They further submitted that under Section 36-A, offences
punishable with imprisonment not exceeding three years, unless triable by a Special Court under

Section 36-AB, must be tried by a Judicial Magistrate First Class (JMFC). The Supreme Court
rejected these contentions, observing that the allegations included misuse of habit-forming drugs
and manipulation during manufacturing, thereby attracting Section 18(a)(vi), which prohibits
manufacture or sale in contravention of Chapter IV or the Rules. Since Section 27(d) prescribes
imprisonment of not less than one year and up to two years, the limitation period under Section
468 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) is three years. The complaint filed within two years
and six months was thus not time-barred. Critically, the Court held that Section 32(2) specifically
mandates that no Court inferior to a Sessions Court shall try offences punishable under Chapter
IV. This provision overrides Section 36-A, which itself excludes offences triable by Sessions Courts.
The committal to the Sessions Court was therefore upheld, and the appeal dismissed.

offences under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 (D&C Act). The bench comprising Justice

manufacturing premises of M/s SBS Biotech in Himachal Pradesh, where the Drug Inspector
alleged non-maintenance of records as mandated under Schedule M and Schedule U of the Drugs
and Cosmetics Rules, 1945. Schedule M prescribes good manufacturing practices and
documentation requirements, while Schedule U specifies particulars to be shown in manufacturing
records. A re-inspection on August 5, 2014, revealed discrepancies in manufacturing, testing, and
distribution records. Following sanction on September 15, 2016, a complaint was filed on February
27, 2017, alleging contraventions of Section 18(a)(vi) read with Rule 74, and Section 22(1)(cca)
read with Section 18-B, punishable under Section 27(d) and Section 28-A. The appellants
contended that mere non-maintenance of records falls under Section 18-B, punishable under

XIV. The Supreme Court of India has established stringent safeguards for convictions based on
circumstantial evidence, where no direct eyewitness testimony exists and guilt must be inferred
from surrounding facts. In the landmark judgment of Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v. State of
Maharashtra, the Court articulated the "Five Golden Principles" or "Panchsheel of Circumstantial
Evidence": (1) circumstances must be fully established, (2) they must be consistent only with the
guilt of the accused, (3) they must be conclusive in nature and tendency, (4) they must exclude
every possible hypothesis except guilt, and (5) there must be a complete chain of evidence with no
missing links. These principles mandate extreme judicial caution because conviction relies on
inference rather than direct observation, creating possibilities for human error, conjecture, and
suspicion masquerading as proof. The First Information Report (FIR), though not substantive
evidence, plays a crucial evidentiary role. Under Section 11 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872,
omissions of important facts in the FIR are relevant in judging witness veracity, as recognized in
Ram Kumar Pandey v. State of Madhya Pradesh. Omissions become particularly serious when
known accused names are absent, crucial facts appear only in later statements, or the FIR
contradicts the prosecution's subsequent narrative. In circumstantial cases, such omissions
significantly weaken the evidentiary chain. Test Identification Parades (TIP), conducted before a
Magistrate during investigation, serve to test a witness's memory and identification capacity. As
clarified in P. Sasikumar v. State, while TIP itself is not substantive evidence, dock identification

in court constitutes substantive evidence. However, when the accused is a stranger to the witness
and no TIP was conducted, dock identification becomes inherently unsafe due to memory
degradation, possible police exposure influencing recognition, and the suggestive nature of
courtroom settings. The "last seen theory" whereby guilt may be inferred if accused and deceased
were last seen together shortly before death requires extreme caution. In State of U.P. v. Satish,
the Court held that the time gap must be so minimal that third-party intervention is effectively
ruled out. This principle was consistently reiterated in Hatti Singh v. State of Haryana, Chattar
Singh v. State of Haryana, and Krishan Kumar v. State of Haryana, where the Court emphasized
that last seen evidence alone is insufficient, requires corroboration, and cannot be stretched
through conjecture or across wide time gaps. Scientific evidence including DNA analysis,
fingerprints, Forensic Science Laboratory (FSL) reports, serology, and ballistics provides objective,
independent verification less prone to human bias. When scientific evidence is neutral or
exculpatory such as DNA mismatches, blood group inconsistencies, or failure to link weapons,
courts cannot ignore these findings and convict on suspicion alone. The fundamental principle,
articulated in Kali Ram v. State of Himachal Pradesh, mandates that when two views are possible
one indicating guilt and another innocence the accused must receive the benefit of doubt.
Suspicion, regardless of strength, cannot substitute proof beyond reasonable doubt, which remains
the immutable standard in criminal law.

Conviction is unsustainable because dock identification without a prior TIP is inherently
unsafe under the P. Sasikumar rule regardless of other corroborative evidence.

Conviction is sustainable because the 20-minute gap satisfies the last seen theory, fingerprints
are scientific evidence, and TIP is only required for strangers.

Conviction is unsustainable because the last seen theory requires independent corroboration
and cannot stand alone as the sole basis for conviction in this case.

Conviction is sustainable because fingerprints constitute conclusive scientific evidence which
legally overrides any procedural defects regarding the witness identification.

content.passageText:
XV. ‘The interpretation of contracts in Indian law follows a structured methodology balancing textual
fidelity with commercial realism. The literal rule serves as the foundational principle, requiring
courts to give contractual terms their plain, grammatical, and ordinary meaning. When language
is clear and unambiguous, courts will not look beyond the text, respecting party autonomy and the
principle of consensus ad idem (meeting of minds). However, the golden rule permits departure
from literal interpretation when it leads to absurd, commercially irrational, or internally
inconsistent outcomes. Courts may adjust meaning sufficiently to avoid absurdity but cannot
rewrite contractual terms to achieve fairness or commercial wisdom.
The purposive approach, borrowed from statutory interpretation, allows courts to examine the
factual matrix and commercial background surrounding the agreement, considering related
documentation, parties' conduct, and the agreement's overall structure. This approach was
articulated in Investors Compensation Scheme Ltd. v. West Bromwich Building Society, where
Lord Hoffmann established that interpretation requires objective understanding as a reasonable
person would have at the time of contracting, considering the matrix of facts available to parties
while excluding prior negotiations and subjective intentions. www.lawpreptutorial.com
The parol evidence rule, codified in Sections 91 and 92 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872,
restricts use of external evidence to contradict clear written terms, as affirmed in Mangala
Waman Karandikar v. Prakash Damodar Ranade. This ensures the written agreement stands as
the final expression of intent. The doctrine of business efficacy permits courts to imply terms
when essential to ensure contracts deliver their intended commercial result, tested through the
officious bystander test—whether both parties would have agreed with "of course" if the term
had been suggested during negotiations. As applied in Mumbai Metropolitan Region Development
Authority v. Unity Infraprojects Ltd., this doctrine gives practical effect to contracts when written
text insufficiently conveys parties' intention, without rewriting agreements. The contra
proferentem rule resolves persistent ambiguity against the drafting party, particularly in
insurance and consumer contracts or where bargaining power is unequal.
The principle of harmonious construction requires reconciling potentially conflicting
provisions within the same contract, ensuring no clause becomes redundant and the document
operates as an internally coherent whole. Courts also apply what may be termed the principle
against disguise: where parties structure agreements to conceal true commercial nature, courts
examine substance over form, looking beyond surface terminology to reveal actual commercial
effect. This principle reflects the judicial posture that legal consequences flow from substance, not
presentation.

XVI. In criminal jurisprudence, the doctrine of mens rea bifurcates into intention and knowledge,
constituting the foundational mental elements requisite for establishing culpability in most penal
offences. Intention denotes the deliberate purpose or conscious design accompanying the
commission of an act, whereas knowledge signifies cognitive awareness of the probable
consequences emanating from such conduct, notwithstanding the absence of desire for the specific
result. Indian criminal law recognizes a hierarchical gradation of mental states, and this
taxonomy materially influences both the characterization of the offence and the quantum of
liability imposed. The Indian Penal Code, 1860 (IPC) distinctly demarcates acts perpetrated
intentionally, knowingly, or with rashness. Culpable homicide as contemplated under Section 299
IPC may be predicated upon either the intention to cause death or knowledge that the act is
imminently likely to cause death, whereas death occasioned by rash or negligent conduct falls
within the ambit of Section 304A IPC. Certain factual matrices, however, obfuscate this doctrinal
distinction. When an act is executed with knowledge that harm may potentially ensue, yet
accompanied by subjective optimism that adverse consequences might be averted, penal liability
may nevertheless crystallize. This principle assumes particular salience where the accused
consciously undertook a calculated risk and the deleterious consequence remained objectively
foreseeable. This interpretive framework ensures that criminal liability is not imposed

XVIII. Prime Minister Narendra Modi Ji’s recent address to the Rajya Sabha was not a statesman’s
summation of governance but a campaign speech delivered from the commanding heights of
power. Ironically, it echoed the very style of politics Modi Ji once rose by condemning. As a
challenger, he criticised governments that mistook dominance for legitimacy, rhetoric for
stewardship, and spectacle for substance. Yet in this parliamentary address, he relied on precisely
those methods, erasing the distinction between campaigning and governing.
Parliament, the republic’s most sacred deliberative institution, was transformed into a rally stage.
This raises a deeper democratic question: what happens when a leader continues to behave like an
insurgent long after becoming sovereign? In parliamentary democracies, the executive’s role is not
to overpower debate but to elevate it. A prime minister is not merely a political combatant but the
custodian of institutional tone, constitutional restraint, and democratic norms.
Modi Ji’s speech moved in the opposite direction. Rather than confronting unemployment,

SECTION I
IL	Supposing that nothing else is "given" as real but our world of desires and passions, that we
cannot sink or rise to any other "reality" but just that of our impulses—for thinking is only a
relation of these impulses to one another:—are we not permitted to make the attempt and to
ask the question whether this which is "given" does not suffice, by means of our counterparts,
for the understanding even of the so-called mechanical (or "material") world? I do not mean as
an illusion, a "semblance," a "representation" (in the Berkeleyan and Schopenhauerian sense),
but as possessing the same degree of reality as our emotions themselves—as a more primitive
form of the world of emotions, in which everything still lies locked in a mighty unity, which
afterwards branches off and develops itself in organic processes (naturally also, refines and
debilitates)—as a kind of instinctive life in which all organic functions, including self-
regulation, assimilation, nutrition, secretion, and change of matter, are still synthetically
united with one another—as a primary form of life?—In the end, it is not only permitted to
make this attempt, it is commanded by the conscience of logical method. Not to assume several
kinds of causality, so long as the attempt to get along with a single one has not been pushed to
its furthest extent (to absurdity, if I may be allowed to say so): that is a morality of method
which one may not repudiate nowadays—it follows "from its definition," as mathematicians
say. The question is ultimately whether we really recognize the will as operating, whether we
believe in the causality of the will; if we do so—and fundamentally our belief in this is just our
belief in causality itself—we must make the attempt to posit hypothetically the causality of the
will as the only causality. "Will" can naturally only operate on "will"—and not on "matter" (not
on "nerves," for instance): in short, the hypothesis must be hazarded, whether will does not
operate on will wherever "effects" are recognized—and whether all mechanical action,
inasmuch as a power operates therein, is not just the power of will, the effect of will. Granted,
finally, that we succeeded in explaining our entire instinctive life as the development and
ramification of one fundamental form of will—namely, the Will to Power, as my thesis puts it;
granted that all organic functions could be traced back to this Will to Power, and that the
solution of the problem of generation and nutrition—it is one problem—could also be found
therein: one would thus have acquired the right to define all active force unequivocally as will
to power. The world seen from within, the world defined and designated according to its
"intelligible character"—it would simply be "Will to Power," and nothing else.
Source: Beyond Good and Evil by Friedrich Nietzsche
Specifically adapted from Section 36 discussing the concept of the “Will to Power.”
The passage in your document is very close to the original philosophical prose, with minimal
modification.

content.passageText:
Til.	Of course, Marx was human and fallible. If "Capital" had never been written, there would still
have been a Socialist movement, and if it could be destroyed by criticism, the Socialist
movement would remain. Socialism is the product of economic conditions, not of a theory or a
book. "Capital" is the intellectual explanation of the genesis of Socialism, and neither its cause
nor an argument for it by which it must be judged. Hence the futility of such missions as that
undertaken by Mr. W. H. Mallock, for example, based upon the assumption that attacks upon
the text of Marx will serve to destroy or seriously hinder the living movement. Like a prophet's
rebuke to these critics, as well as to those within the ranks of the Socialist movement who
would make of the words of Marx and Engels fetters to bind the movement to a dogma, come
the words of Engels, published recently, letters in which he writes vigorously to his friend
Sorge concerning the working-class movement in England and America. Of his compatriots,
the handful of German Socialist exiles in America, who sought to make the American workers
swallow a mass of ill-digested Marxian theory, he writes, "The Germans have never
understood how to apply themselves from their theory to the lever which could set the
American masses in motion; to a great extent they do not understand the theory itself and
treat it in a doctrinaire and dogmatic fashion.... It is a credo to them, not a guide to action."
And again, "Our theory is not a dogma, but the exposition of a process of evolution, and that
process involves several successive phases." Of the English movement he writes, "And here an
instinctive Socialism is more and more taking possession of the masses which, fortunately, is
opposed to all distinct formulation according to the dogmas of one or the other so-called
organizations," and again, he condemns "the bringing down of the Marxian theory of
development to a rigid orthodoxy." The critics who hope to destroy the Socialist movement of
to-day by stringing together mistaken predictions of Marx and Engels, or who think that
Socialism is losing its grip because it is adjusting its expressions to the changed conditions

which the progress of fifty years has brought about, utterly mistake the character of the
movement. In its abandonment of the errors of Marx it is most truly Marxian—because it is
expressing life instead of repeating dogma.
Source: Socialism: A Summary and Interpretation of Socialist Principles
The passage contains direct references to Engels’ letters to Sorge and discussions about
doctrinaire Marxism.

IV.	The hotel emerged through the snow like a structure abandoned by time itself. Perched deep
within the Alps, the building had once served as a sanatorium for tuberculosis patients, and
despite its expensive renovations, fragments of that history remained untouched. Rusted iron
railings lined the balconies, faded medical charts hung behind glass frames, and the corridors
carried a strange stillness that made every movement seem intrusive.

V.	The Union Cabinet recently cleared a legislative proposal aimed at revising an existing law
governing the sanctioned strength of the country's apex judicial institution. The proposed
amendment seeks to expand the court’s adjudicatory capacity by increasing the number of
judges, with the objective of addressing growing judicial demands and improving the efficiency
of case disposal.
It has been widely welcomed by members of the legal fraternity, who described it as a timely
step to deal with rising pendency and growing litigation before the apex court.
Many legal experts believe that increasing the capacity of higher courts can help them
function more effectively. A larger number of judges may allow courts to hear more cases,
devote greater attention to important constitutional matters, and reduce the burden on
individual judges. This, in turn, could contribute to quicker disposal of cases and a more
responsive justice system.
However, former Union Law Secretary PK Malhotra said that simply increasing the number of
judges may not bring major judicial reforms. He suggested that the government should
consider setting up regional Courts of Appeal so that the Supreme Court can focus mainly on
constitutional matters.
Overall, while legal experts have largely welcomed the Centre's decision, many believe that
increasing the number of judges must be accompanied by wider judicial reforms to effectively
tackle delays and pendency in the justice delivery system.
Source: Adapted from "President Murmu Approves Increasing Supreme Court Judge Strength,"
The Hindu.

VI.	For much of the space age, launching rockets and building space technology were activities
largely reserved for national space agencies. The high costs, technological complexity, and
risks associated with space missions made it difficult for private companies to participate
meaningfully in the sector. However, this situation has begun to change as advances in
technology, greater access to investment, and supportive policy reforms have opened new
opportunities for private enterprises.
India's space sector has experienced a particularly significant transformation in recent years.
A growing number of start-ups are developing launch vehicles, satellite technologies, and
other space-based solutions. Their emergence reflects increasing confidence in the commercial
potential of the country's space ecosystem and demonstrates how innovation-driven businesses
can contribute to fields traditionally dominated by the government.
One notable milestone in this journey was achieved by Skyroot Aerospace, a Hyderabad-based
space technology company, which became one of the few Indian private space firms to attain
unicorn status after crossing a valuation of more than one billion dollars. Founded by former
scientists and engineers from the Indian space sector, the company has focused on developing
launch vehicles for small satellites. Its rise has been viewed as an important indicator of
investor confidence in India's expanding private space industry.
The achievement extends beyond financial valuation. It signals growing global interest in
India's capabilities in advanced technology and aerospace innovation. Supporters argue that
such developments can attract further investment, generate high-skilled employment, and
encourage collaboration between government agencies, research institutions, and private
companies.

As the global space economy continues to expand, the success of companies like Skyroot
Aerospace highlights the increasing role that private enterprise can play in shaping the future
of space exploration and commercial space activities.
Source: Indian Space-Tech Company Skyroot Aerospace Becomes Unicorn, THE HINDU (May
2026)

largely reserved for national space agencies. The high costs, technological complexity, and
risks associated with space missions made it difficult for private companies to participate
meaningfully in the sector. However, this situation has begun to change as advances in
technology, greater access to investment, and supportive policy reforms have opened new
opportunities for private enterprises.

A growing number of start-ups are developing launch vehicles, satellite technologies, and
other space-based solutions. Their emergence reflects increasing confidence in the commercial
potential of the country's space ecosystem and demonstrates how innovation-driven businesses
can contribute to fields traditionally dominated by the government.

unicorn status after crossing a valuation of more than one billion dollars. Founded by former
scientists and engineers from the Indian space sector, the company has focused on developing
launch vehicles for small satellites. Its rise has been viewed as an important indicator of
investor confidence in India's expanding private space industry.

India's capabilities in advanced technology and aerospace innovation. Supporters argue that
such developments can attract further investment, generate high-skilled employment, and
encourage collaboration between government agencies, research institutions, and private
companies.

Aerospace highlights the increasing role that private enterprise can play in shaping the future
of space exploration and commercial space activities.

VII. The global governing body of the Olympic Movement has approved a revised participation
framework for female sporting categories. Under the new policy, eligibility for women's events
at major international competitions will be determined through a uniform verification
mechanism. "Eligibility for any female category event at the Olympic Games or any other IOC
event, including individual and team sports, is now limited to biological females," the
International Olympic Committee said, to be determined by a mandatory gene test once in an
athlete's career.
It is unclear how many, if any, transgender women are competing at an Olympic level. No
woman who transitioned from being born male competed at the 2024 Paris Summer Games,
though weightlifter Laurel Hubbard did at the Tokyo Olympics in 2021 without winning a
medal. The eligibility policy that will apply from the LA Olympics in July 2028 "protects
fairness, safety and integrity in the female category," the IOC said.
After an executive board meeting, the International Olympic Committee published a 10-page
policy document which also restricts female athletes such as two-time Olympic champion
runner Caster Semenya with medical conditions known as differences in sex development, or
DSD.
The IOC said its research included "in-depth individual interviews with impacted athletes
from around the world." The expert group agreed the current gene test is "the most accurate
and least intrusive method currently available." The saliva, cheek swab or blood sample
screens for "the SRY gene, a segment of DNA typically found on the Y chromosome that
initiates male sex development in utero and indicates the presence of testes/testicles."
Source: Kyle Feldscher, Transgender Women Athletes Banned from Olympics Following New
IOC Guidelines, CNN (Mar. 26, 2026)

content.passageText:
VIII. From the very beginning, women were active participants in the events which brought about
many important changes in French society. They hoped that their involvement would
pressurise the revolutionary government to introduce measures to improve their lives. Most
women of the Third Estate had to work for a living. They worked as seamstresses or
laundresses, sold flowers, fruits and vegetables in the market, or were employed as domestic
servants in the houses of prosperous people.
Most women did not have access to education or job training. Only daughters of nobles or
wealthier members of the Third Estate could study at a convent, after which their families
arranged a marriage for them. Working women also had to care for their families. They cooked
food, fetched water, queued up for bread, and looked after children. Despite carrying out these
responsibilities, their wages were lower than those of men.
In order to discuss and voice their interests, women started their own political clubs and
newspapers. About sixty women's clubs came up in different French cities. The Society of
Revolutionary and Republican Women was the most famous among them. One of their main
demands was that women should enjoy the same political rights as men. Women were
disappointed that the Constitution of 1791 reduced them to passive citizens. They demanded
the right to vote, to be elected to the Assembly, and to hold political office. They believed that
only then would their interests be represented in the new government.
In the early years, the revolutionary government introduced several laws that helped improve
the lives of women. Along with the creation of state schools, schooling was made compulsory
for all girls. Fathers could no longer force their daughters into marriage against their will.
Marriage became a contract entered into freely and registered under civil law. Divorce was
made legal and could be applied for by both women and men. Women could now train for jobs,
become artists, or run small businesses.
Source: Adapted from India and the Contemporary World-I (History), Class IX, Chapter 1: The
French Revolution, NCERT

IX.	In the first major legislative loss for the Modi government since it came to power in 2014, the
Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026, seeking to advance reservation of 33% seats for
women in an expanded Lok Sabha and state Assemblies and facilitate delimitation of
constituencies, was defeated in Lok Sabha Friday evening.
Of the 528 members present in the House, 298 voted in favour of the Bill and 230 opposed it,
the result well short of the two-thirds majority needed for a Constitutional amendment Bill to
clear the House.
The amended women's quota Bill was put to vote after a marathon two-day debate during
which Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Home Minister Amit Shah urged members to
support the proposed legislation, and cautioned the Opposition that women of the country
were watching their intent and would not forgive them if they were denied reservation.
The Opposition, in turn, accused the government of using the women's reservation issue to
push for a delimitation exercise to help the BJP by redrawing the country's electoral map and
adversely impacting the representation of southern states in Lok Sabha. The rejected bill
sought to fast-track the implementation of women's reservation and permit delimitation

without waiting for a fresh Census. It aimed to amend provisions linked to the Nari Shakti
Vandan Adhiniyam, which provides 33 per cent reservation for women in the Lok Sabha and
state legislatures.
Source: Adapted from "Women's Quota Bill Defeated in Lok Sabha; Fails to Get Two-Thirds
Majority,” The New Indian Express (Apr. 17, 2026)

In the event of a deadlock between the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha over the passage of a
Constitution Amendment Bill, which of the following constitutional courses of action is
available?

The President can summon a joint sitting of both Houses under Article 108 to resolve the
deadlock.

The Bill is deemed passed if the Lok Sabha passes it a second time with a three-fourths
majority.

The bill is automatically referred to the Supreme Court for arbitration under its original
jurisdiction.

The Bill lapses, as there is no provision for a joint sitting for a Constitution Amendment
Bill.

content.passageText:
X.	It is impossible not to smile darkly when the results of a G2 summit are discrepant readouts:
It seems that presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping cannot agree on what was agreed on
during their recent talks. The good news: They seem not to be colluding to divide up the world
into new spheres of influence. But global instability is not about to diminish.
Today, international trade is increasingly shaped by geopolitical rivalries, national security
concerns, and strategic competition among major powers. Governments are no longer viewing
trade solely as a means of economic exchange; it is also being used as an instrument of foreign
policy and national strategy. This shift has exposed the limitations of a trade framework that
often treats economic issues in isolation from broader political realities.
At the same time, several longstanding concerns of developing countries remain unresolved.
Questions relating to equitable development, market access, and the unequal distribution of
gains from globalization continue to feature prominently in international trade discussions.
Meanwhile, new challenges have emerged, including concerns about supply-chain
vulnerabilities, technological dependence, cybersecurity risks, and the environmental
consequences of economic growth. These issues often extend beyond the traditional mandate of
trade institutions but nevertheless influence trade relations in significant ways.
Many observers argue that if the WTO is to remain effective, it must acknowledge the political
forces shaping global commerce rather than treating them as external factors. Recognizing
differences in national priorities, accommodating diverse developmental needs, and
encouraging more flexible forms of cooperation may help the organization adapt to a rapidly
changing world. Ultimately, the future of the multilateral trading system may depend on its
ability to balance economic objectives with the political realities that increasingly influence
international trade.
Source: Amrita Narlikar, For WTO to Matter, It Needs to Recognise Politics Behind Trade,
INDIAN EXPRESS (May 19, 2026)

X.	It is impossible not to smile darkly when the results of a G2 summit are discrepant readouts:
It seems that presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping cannot agree on what was agreed on
during their recent talks. The good news: They seem not to be colluding to divide up the world
into new spheres of influence. But global instability is not about to diminish.
Today, international trade is increasingly shaped by geopolitical rivalries, national security
concerns, and strategic competition among major powers. Governments are no longer viewing
trade solely as a means of economic exchange; it is also being used as an instrument of foreign
policy and national strategy. This shift has exposed the limitations of a trade framework that
often treats economic issues in isolation from broader political realities.
At the same time, several longstanding concerns of developing countries remain unresolved.
Questions relating to equitable development, market access, and the unequal distribution of
gains from globalization continue to feature prominently in international trade discussions.
Meanwhile, new challenges have emerged, including concerns about supply-chain
vulnerabilities, technological dependence, cybersecurity risks, and the environmental
consequences of economic growth. These issues often extend beyond the traditional mandate of
trade institutions but nevertheless influence trade relations in significant ways.
Many observers argue that if the WTO is to remain effective, it must acknowledge the political
forces shaping global commerce rather than treating them as external factors. Recognizing
differences in national priorities, accommodating diverse developmental needs, and
encouraging more flexible forms of cooperation may help the organization adapt to a rapidly
changing world. Ultimately, the future of the multilateral trading system may depend on its
ability to balance economic objectives with the political realities that increasingly influence
international trade.
Source: Amrita Narlikar, For WTO to Matter, It Needs to Recognise Politics Behind Trade,

XII. The Supreme Court’s judgment in J&K Economic Reconstruction Agency v. Rash Builders
India Private Limited revisited the distinction between the “seat” and “venue” of arbitration
and clarified how this distinction determines the supervisory jurisdiction of courts under the
Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. The dispute arose from infrastructure contracts
executed in Jammu and Kashmir between the Jammu and Kashmir Economic Reconstruction
Agency (JKERA) and Rash Builders India Pvt. Ltd. After disagreements concerning
contractual claims, arbitration proceedings were initiated.
Initially, the High Court of Jammu and Kashmir appointed a sole arbitrator. Subsequently, by
an order dated 26 March 2016, the arbitral tribunal recorded that, with the consent of both
parties, Srinagar would be the “seat” of arbitration while New Delhi would merely function as
the “venue” for conducting hearings. The proceedings were later conducted in New Delhi for
convenience, and the arbitral award was also pronounced there.
After the award was delivered, JKERA filed a petition under Section 34 of the Arbitration and
Conciliation Act before the Jammu and Kashmir High Court seeking to challenge the award.
However, the High Court returned the petition on the ground that since hearings were

conducted and the award was rendered in New Delhi, courts in Delhi alone possessed
jurisdiction. JKERA challenged this conclusion before the Supreme Court.
The Supreme Court observed that arbitration law consistently recognizes a distinction
between “seat” and “venue.” According to the Court, the seat of arbitration constitutes the
juridical home of the arbitration and determines which court exercises supervisory jurisdiction
over arbitral proceedings. The venue, by contrast, is merely a geographically convenient place
where hearings may be conducted. Therefore, the mere fact that hearings occur or an award is
delivered at a particular location does not automatically transfer jurisdiction to courts situated
there.
The Court emphasized that once parties expressly designate a seat of arbitration, courts at
that place alone possess exclusive jurisdiction over arbitration-related proceedings, including
challenges to arbitral awards. Such designation operates similarly to an exclusive jurisdiction
clause in commercial contracts. The Court further held that the seat remains fixed and
immutable unless the parties expressly agree to alter it later. www.lawpreptutorial.com
Applying these principles, the Supreme Court held that Srinagar remained the juridical seat
because the parties had expressly agreed to it. The Court rejected the respondent’s argument
that the award mentioning New Delhi as the “place of arbitration” changed the seat. According
to the Court, stray recitals in an arbitral award cannot override the express agreement of
parties. Consequently, the Supreme Court set aside the High Court’s order and restored
JKERA’s Section 34 proceedings before the Jammu and Kashmir High Court. The judgment
reaffirmed party autonomy, certainty in arbitral procedure, and the central importance of the
juridical seat in determining court jurisdiction.
Source: https://www.verdictum.in/supreme-court /jk-economic-reconstruction-agency-v-rash-
builders-india-private-limited-2026-insc-368-seat-venue-arbitration- 1612216

XIII. The doctrine of constructive res judicata is an important extension of the principle of res
judicata embodied under Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (CPC). While the
traditional rule of res judicata bars the re-litigation of issues that have already been directly
and substantially decided between the same parties, constructive res judicata prevents parties
from raising matters in subsequent proceedings that they “might and ought” to have raised in
earlier litigation. The doctrine is primarily incorporated through Explanation IV to Section 11
CPC and is closely connected with Order II Rule 2 of the CPC.
The rationale behind the doctrine is based upon public policy, judicial economy, and the need
to ensure finality in litigation. Courts seek to prevent parties from splitting claims or
withholding grounds strategically in order to initiate multiple rounds of litigation over the
same dispute. The principle is therefore intended to protect opposing parties from repeated
harassment and to prevent wastage of judicial time. The Supreme Court has repeatedly
emphasized that litigation must eventually attain finality, since endless challenges undermine
public confidence in the judicial process.
Recently, the Supreme Court examined the doctrine while considering a dispute concerning
property rights where a respondent attempted to claim reliefs in a later suit that could and
should have been sought in an earlier proceeding itself. The Court observed that the dispute
regarding the parties’ rights already existed at the time of the first suit, and therefore all
connected reliefs ought to have been claimed together. Since the respondent was fully aware of
the rival claim during the earlier proceedings, the subsequent suit was barred by constructive
res judicata and by the principles underlying Order II Rule 2 CPC. The Court held that parties
cannot be permitted to re-agitate issues by merely altering the form of relief sought in later
litigation.
The doctrine has also been applied beyond ordinary civil suits. In M. Nagabhushana v. State of
Karnataka (2011), the Supreme Court clarified that constructive res judicata may apply even
to writ petitions. The Court reasoned that litigants cannot repeatedly invoke constitutional
remedies on grounds that could reasonably have been urged earlier. However, courts have also

recognized that the doctrine should not be applied mechanically in exceptional situations
involving changed circumstances, continuing violations, or issues affecting personal liberty.
Thus, constructive res judicata represents a balance between two competing concerns:
ensuring fairness to litigants while also preserving certainty, consistency, and finality in
judicial proceedings. The doctrine discourages fragmented litigation and promotes efficient
administration of justice by compelling parties to present their entire case at the earliest
available opportunity.

constructive-res-judicata-if-plaintiff-omitted-it-in-earlier-injunction-suit-where-title-was-

despite knowing that B is occupying the property. After losing the first suit, A files another
suit seeking possession on the basis of the same title dispute. Applying the doctrine discussed

The second suit is barred because A ought to have claimed all connected reliefs in the first

XIII. The doctrine of constructive res judicata is an important extension of the principle of res
judicata embodied under Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (CPC). While the
traditional rule of res judicata bars the re-litigation of issues that have already been directly
and substantially decided between the same parties, constructive res judicata prevents parties
from raising matters in subsequent proceedings that they “might and ought” to have raised in
earlier litigation. The doctrine is primarily incorporated through Explanation IV to Section 11
CPC and is closely connected with Order II Rule 2 of the CPC.
The rationale behind the doctrine is based upon public policy, judicial economy, and the need
to ensure finality in litigation. Courts seek to prevent parties from splitting claims or
withholding grounds strategically in order to initiate multiple rounds of litigation over the
same dispute. The principle is therefore intended to protect opposing parties from repeated
harassment and to prevent wastage of judicial time. The Supreme Court has repeatedly
emphasized that litigation must eventually attain finality, since endless challenges undermine
public confidence in the judicial process.
Recently, the Supreme Court examined the doctrine while considering a dispute concerning
property rights where a respondent attempted to claim reliefs in a later suit that could and
should have been sought in an earlier proceeding itself. The Court observed that the dispute
regarding the parties’ rights already existed at the time of the first suit, and therefore all
connected reliefs ought to have been claimed together. Since the respondent was fully aware of
the rival claim during the earlier proceedings, the subsequent suit was barred by constructive
res judicata and by the principles underlying Order II Rule 2 CPC. The Court held that parties
cannot be permitted to re-agitate issues by merely altering the form of relief sought in later
litigation.
The doctrine has also been applied beyond ordinary civil suits. In M. Nagabhushana v. State of
Karnataka (2011), the Supreme Court clarified that constructive res judicata may apply even
to writ petitions. The Court reasoned that litigants cannot repeatedly invoke constitutional
remedies on grounds that could reasonably have been urged earlier. However, courts have also

recognized that the doctrine should not be applied mechanically in exceptional situations
involving changed circumstances, continuing violations, or issues affecting personal liberty.
Thus, constructive res judicata represents a balance between two competing concerns:
ensuring fairness to litigants while also preserving certainty, consistency, and finality in
judicial proceedings. The doctrine discourages fragmented litigation and promotes efficient
administration of justice by compelling parties to present their entire case at the earliest
available opportunity.

petition is dismissed. Later, P files another writ petition challenging the same notification on
constitutional grounds that existed and were known during the first petition. Which of the
following best reflects the reasoning in the passage?

The second writ petition is maintainable because constitutional grounds can never be
barred.
The second petition is maintainable because writ jurisdiction is discretionary.

Constructive res judicata applies only to civil suits under the CPC and never to writ

The second writ petition may be barred because constructive res judicata may apply to writ

The second petition may be maintainable because courts recognize exceptions involving

The second petition is barred because all future challenges must be raised in the first

XIV. In a landmark development, the Supreme Court of India has held that the right to trauma
care is an integral part of the right to life guaranteed under Article 21 of the Constitution. The
ruling, delivered in Save LIFE Foundation v. Union of India by a bench of Justices J.K.
Maheshwari and Atul S. Chandurkar, builds upon an earlier 2025 directive in 8. Rajaseekaran
v. Union of India, where the Court ruled that access to trauma care during the golden hour is
not simply a matter of policy but a constitutional right under Article 21.
The "golden hour" refers to the first 60 minutes after a serious injury—the period when rapid
intervention can be the difference between life and death. The Court observed that a systemic

intervention, creation of a uniform framework for trauma care, building public awareness,
standardization of first aid skills and proper Good Samaritan laws are essential to protect this
right.
This jurisprudence rests on robust precedent. In Paschim Banga Khet Mazdoor Samity (1996),
the Court held that denial of emergency care violates Article 21 and directed states to
establish referral protocols, designated hospitals, and budgetary measures, while SaveLIFE
Foundation v. Union of India (2016) gave binding force to Good Samaritan protections,
encouraging bystander assistance.
In its recent directions, the Court ordered all States and Union Territories to operationalise
within three months one helpline number '112' for emergency responses and establish
functional good samaritan grievance redressal system. It further directed that all states and
UTs that have not yet adopted the cashless treatment of road accident victims scheme, 2025 —
PM RAHAT, shall take necessary steps to fully operationalise the said schemes within a
period of three months. The Court also permitted the Centre to issue a medical rescue protocol
for trauma cases within three months, and directed all States and Union Territories to
operationalise the same within three months thereafter.
Emphasising the urgency, the Court noted that in cases of road accidents, every minute
without medical intervention significantly narrows the scope for survival, adding that the
initial response and first aid is perhaps the most crucial stage of care. States were also
directed to furnish periodic compliance reports by organising monthly meetings and uploading
the minutes on the concerned portals.
This evolving framework transforms trauma care from a matter of administrative discretion
into an enforceable fundamental right, reinforcing the State's positive obligation to protect life
through accessible, time-sensitive emergency medical care.

directs-to-integrate-emergency-helplines-into-112-implement-pm-rahat-good-samaritan-scheme-

content.questionText:
A State government, four months after the Court's directions, has integrated helpline 112 but
has neither held the required monthly meetings nor uploaded any minutes, arguing that
integrating the helpline alone fulfils its obligation. Based strictly on the directions described in
the passage, which assessment is most accurate?
options:
The State has fully complied, since helpline integration was the principal direction and
reporting was optional

The State has complied with the substantive direction but the reporting obligation was
merely advisory

The State has not fully complied, because furnishing periodic compliance reports through
monthly meetings with uploaded minutes was itself a directed obligation

The State's compliance cannot be assessed until the Centre issues the medical rescue
protocol
content.explanation: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: The State has not fully complied, because furnishing periodic compliance reports through monthly meetings with uploaded minutes was itself a directed obligation. Accordingly, option C is the keyed legal result.

XV. In a significant ruling on personal liberty and individual autonomy, the Kerala High Court
has held that parents cannot invoke the writ of habeas corpus merely because they disapprove
of their adult daughters’ decision to join a religious congregation and lead a life of celibacy.
The case, Joju George and Ors. v. State of Kerala and Ors. (2026), was decided by a Division
Bench comprising Justice A.K. Jayasankaran Nambiar and Justice Jobin Sebastian of the
Kerala High Court.
The petition was filed by three parents alleging that their daughters, aged 21, 26 and 30, were
being illegally detained by members of a religious congregation known as the Monastery of
Holy Ruah (MHR). According to the petitioners, their daughters had joined the congregation
when it was recognised by the Archdiocese of Thrissur. However, after the Archdiocese
dissolved the congregation in 2023, the parents claimed that their daughters continued to
remain there under coercion.
The petitioners argued that parental guidance and authority over children should not be
brushed aside merely because the children had attained majority, contending that courts
should intervene where decisions taken by adult children were immature or influenced. The
Court rejected this reasoning. It noted that police enquiries revealed that the daughters
themselves signed statements affirming that they were voluntarily continuing with the
congregation. Accordingly, the Court held that parental disagreement could not justify judicial
intervention through habeas corpus.
A central theme of the judgment was individual autonomy. The Bench observed that the
choice of the alleged detenus with regard to their beliefs or the congregation that they must
join is a matter that rests exclusively within the private domain of the individual concerned,
warning that interference by the State in such matters would have a chilling effect on the
exercise of constitutional freedoms by the individual concerned. The Court cautioned that, as
"sentinels on the qui vive", this Court must tread with caution when called upon to issue writs
in the nature of Habeas Corpus alleging illegal detention.
In its concluding observation, the Bench held that the mere disgruntlement of a parent with
the decision of his adult daughter, who has chosen a life of celibacy by responding to the call of
the Divine, cannot be the basis for the issuance of a writ of Habeas Corpus. The ruling
reinforces a broader judicial trend in India protecting the autonomy of adults to make personal
choices regarding faith and lifestyle, free from parental or State coercion.

kerala-high-court-dismisses-habeas-corpus-plea-by-parents

The writ would be granted, because rejecting parental authority leaves the "immaturity"

The matter would be remanded for the parents to prove majority

The writ would still be refused, because the Court located the choice within the

XVI. The Constitution (One Hundred and Thirty-First Amendment) Bill, 2026 was introduced in
Lok Sabha on 16 April 2026 by Arjun Ram Meghwal, the Minister of Law, during a special
parliamentary session. It targeted Articles 81, 82, and 334A of the Constitution, addressing
two long-pending issues: the expansion of the Lok Sabha and the operationalisation of
women's reservation.
The Bill proposed that the maximum number of seats in Lok Sabha will be increased from 550
to 850, with up to 815 members from States and 35 from Union Territories. Equally
significant, it sought to amend the constitutional provision that the allocation of seats to states
in Lok Sabha will be based on the 1971 census, until the first census after 2026. Instead, the
Bill authorised Parliament to pass a law to determine when delimitation will be undertaken,
and which census will be used. Through the companion Delimitation Bill, 2026, the latest
published census — effectively the 2011 census — would govern the next delimitation.
The Bill's second principal object was to fast-track women's reservation. The 106th
Constitutional Amendment, 2023 (Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam): Providing 33%
reservation for women in Lok Sabha and State Assemblies, came into force on 16th April 2026.
However, its actual implementation is deferred because Article 334A links it to a delimitation
exercise after the next Census (post-2027), making it unlikely to take effect before around

2034. The 131st Amendment Bill sought to delink reservation from the post-2026 census so
that the women's quota could become effective from the 2029 general elections.
The redistributive effect of using the 2011 census would be considerable. As PRS noted, Tamil
Nadu's seats will come down from 39 to 32, and Kerala from 20 to 15. Uttar Pradesh will see
an increase from 80 to 89, Bihar from 40 to 46, and Rajasthan from 25 to 30. This sparked
sharp federal concerns from southern states about diminished representation despite better
demographic performance. www.lawpreptutorial.com
The Bill ultimately failed. On 17th April 2026, with 298 votes in favour and 230 votes against
the bill, it secured a simple majority but fell short of the special majority required under
Article 368. The Opposition Leaders argued the Bill was an attack on the Constitution because
it linked women's rights to a controversial delimitation process that could alter India's
political structure. Its defeat leaves the women's quota tied to the post-2026 census timeline
and reopens the larger question of how India will balance population-based representation
with federal equity.
Source: https://prsindia.org/billtrack/the-constitution-131st-amendment-bill-2026
content.questionText:
A constitutional scholar argues that the 131st Amendment Bill, even if it had been enacted,
would not by itself have implemented women's reservation from 2029 — it required something
more. Based strictly on the passage, this argument is:
options:
Wrong, because the 131st Amendment Bill alone was self-executing and required no
further legislative step

Wrong, because the women's quota had already become operational on 16 April 2026 with
the 106th Amendment coming into force

Correct, because the operationalisation depended on a delimitation exercise governed by
the companion Delimitation Bill, 2026, under which the latest published census would
apply

Correct, because the Rajya Sabha alone could implement reservation, the Lok Sabha being
incompetent
content.explanation: Applying the rule stated in the passage to the facts in the question leads to this conclusion: Correct, because the operationalisation depended on a delimitation exercise governed by the companion Delimitation Bill, 2026, under which the latest published census would apply. Accordingly, option C is the keyed legal result.

XIX. Can a society genuinely claim to oppose dowry while continuing to treat marriage as the
highest marker of respectability? What would it mean to respond to dowry deaths not with
fleeting outrage, but with the courage to imagine different ways of living and belonging? It is
almost always the most extreme forms of violence that disturb the public conscience. Images
spread, testimonies emerge, anger builds, and demands for justice grow louder. Grief appears
collective briefly. Yet the moment passes, almost as predictably. Outrage fades while the social
world that produces such violence remains largely unchanged and even celebrated. Marriage
continues to be presented as aspiration, security, and inevitability, even as financial
transactions surrounding it stay deeply normalised. Dowry may be publicly condemned in
principle, yet it is quietly repackaged through the language of gifts, family honour, or the
assumption that a man, as primary earner, deserves material compensation. Weddings
function as performances of social worth, where financial display is not merely tolerated but
actively admired. Conversations about daughters still carry the language of burden and
responsibility, revealing how deeply marriage remains tied to economic and social anxieties.
Marital violence, therefore, cannot be understood as an exception alone; it grows from a
structure whose underlying logic society continuously justifies. Women enter marriage under

deeply unequal conditions, more likely to give up careers, absorb unpaid care work, and bear
the greater burden of maintaining family harmony. The expectation of sacrifice remains
attached to women, even when softened through the language of compromise or culture. This
is perhaps the central limitation of outrage: it allows society to condemn violence without
examining the conditions that make it normal. Violence is treated as the moral failure of
certain individuals, rather than as a symptom of a social order in which marriage remains tied
to economic exchange, gendered labour, and the preservation of caste hierarchies. Marriage
has historically functioned as far more than a personal relationship. It has operated
simultaneously as an economic arrangement, a mechanism for preserving social boundaries,
and a system through which families negotiate status and security. Financial transaction,
therefore, does not appear accidental to marriage; it is embedded within its very logic. The
violence is not confined to visible brutality alone. It is present in quieter pressures: the social
anxiety surrounding unmarried women, the normalisation of women's endless adjustment as
virtue, and the absence of legitimate alternatives. What society lacks is not simply better laws
or louder condemnation, but the imagination to envision ways of living in which dignity,
belonging, and security do not depend upon marriage.

has historically functioned as far more than a personal relationship. It has operated
simultaneously as an economic arrangement, a mechanism for preserving social boundaries,
and a system through which families negotiate status and security. Financial transaction,
therefore, does not appear accidental to marriage; it is embedded within its very logic. The
violence is not confined to visible brutality alone. It is present in quieter pressures: the social
anxiety surrounding unmarried women, the normalisation of women's endless adjustment as
virtue, and the absence of legitimate alternatives. What society lacks is not simply better laws
or louder condemnation, but the imagination to envision ways of living in which dignity,
belonging, and security do not depend upon marriage.

encounter food as a packaged product with little awareness of its origins. Traditional markets
make the process visible and encourage a more honest relationship with what people eat. This
visibility may not appeal to everyone, yet it fosters awareness rather than detachment.
Conversations about prices, quality and daily life create relationships that extend beyond
commerce. Large retail complexes often provide convenience but rarely foster the same social
bonds. A society benefits when citizens understand the labour and the resources involved in
bringing food to their tables.

engagement and better collective decision-making around agricultural and environmental
policies.

relationships.

XXIV. Direction for Questions 106: Freedom might be priceless but incarceration comes at a cost.
Hyderabad’s Chanchalguda Central Jail now allows citizens to spend 24 hours locked inside a
real prison cell for a price. The aim is to build awareness about prison discipline and drive
home the value of personal freedoms. While it can be argued that being deprived of basic
liberties for a day can prove illuminating, one must ask whether it will make a stark
difference. After all, Indians have been losing liberties — the freedom to choose what to wear,
what to eat, who to marry and so on — for a while now and that does not seem to have
impressed upon them the significance of being free.

Hyderabad joined after the completion of the first year. NLU Jodhpur joined six months after
NALSAR Hyderabad entered the consortium. NLU Bhopal joined after the completion of the
second year. At the conclusion of the project, the consortium generated %4.02 crore through
licensing agreements and commercialization of research outputs. The revenue was distributed
among participating universities according to their effective contribution ratio.
